**Short answer:** Promising to stop and fixing it probably won't work here. Your letter says the lease is terminated and gives you 7 days to leave. It does not offer a chance to fix the problem. Florida law lets a landlord send that kind of letter when there is a repeat problem after a written warning. Your January 15 warning and the March 20 party fit that pattern. The letter alone doesn't put you out. Your landlord still needs a court case to make you leave, and it can't lock you out or shut off utilities.

Has your landlord taken any rent from you since the March 20 party, including any payment through the portal? If so, how much and when?

DETAILS

### Is this a "fix it" letter or a "lease is over" letter?
- Your letter says the lease is "terminated effective immediately" and gives you "7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate." That is the "lease over" kind (83.56(2)(a)).
- A "fix it" letter would say you must correct the problem within 7 days or the lease will end (83.56(2)(b)). Yours doesn't say that, so fixing the problem is not a right under this letter.
- Stopping the parties now is still a good idea. It doesn't undo this notice.

### Is the landlord allowed to skip the chance to fix?
- The statute allows a "lease over" notice when there is "a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)).
- It also lists "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance" as conduct that gets no chance to fix (83.56(2)(a)).
- You got a written warning on January 15 about loud parties after midnight. The new party was on March 20, and the letter says it was after midnight again.
- 12 months from the warning runs to about January 15, 2027, and that date has not passed. March 20 falls inside that window.
- The statute doesn't define "similar" or "unreasonable disturbance." Both look like a fit here, because the warning and the new event are both about loud parties after midnight.
- Your lease also bans this. Section 11 says you and your guests must "keep noise at a level that does not disturb other residents," and "quiet hours are 10:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m."
- You are responsible for guests too. The law requires you to make people you allow in the home behave so they don't disturb neighbors (83.52(7)).

### Was the letter delivered properly, and what does it say?
- The manager handed it to you on March 23. The statute allows "delivering a true copy" (83.56(4)).
- Delivery by hand also fits lease section 8, which says notices go "to the apartment while Tenant lives there."
- The letter says what you did (a loud party after midnight on March 20) and cites the January 15 warning. It also gives 7 days.
- Counting from March 23, the 7 days end March 30. That date has not passed.
- The letter's wording matches the statute's suggested form, so I don't see a flaw in it. I can't say a court would agree.

### Do I have to be out on March 30?
- The notice does not remove you by itself. "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or if you give up the home or abandon it.
- The landlord may not change the locks or otherwise block your access. It "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device." (83.67(2)).
- If it locks you out or cuts a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees." (83.67(6)).
- Don't ignore the letter, though. It starts the 7-day count, and if you stay, your landlord can sue. No case has been filed.
- If you stay and lose, the loser can owe the winner's court costs (83.59(4)), and the winner may also recover attorney fees (83.48). Your landlord may also ask for double rent for the time you stay (83.58). Whether double rent applies when a notice ended the lease, rather than the term running out, is not settled.
- If you are sued, you can only defend the case if you pay the rent into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within 5 days (not counting weekends and holidays). The 5 days count from when you are served (83.56(5)(b), 83.60(2)). The summons will state this requirement. Missing it means you lose your defenses and the court must order you out right away.

### Could the landlord have given up its right by taking rent?
- If your landlord took a full month's rent after it knew about the problem, it may have given up the right to end the lease over that party (83.56(5)(a)).
- Taking only part of a month's rent does not count as giving up the right.
- Rent you paid before March 20 wouldn't count, since the landlord didn't know yet. That is why I'm asking about rent paid since then.

### Is it settled whether a late promise or fix could still help?
- Under this kind of notice, the statute gives no right to fix. A promise to stop does not change what the notice says.
- You can still raise problems with the notice if you are sued. Whether a flaw would end a case is for a court.
- Your landlord could choose to accept a promise, but nothing in the statute requires it. If it does, get that agreement in writing. Lease section 10 says changes to the lease must be in a writing signed by both sides.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded notice_received_violation. Its instructions:

# Notice of a violation

Rests on 83.56(2), (4), (5), and (6) (the notice and how it reaches the tenant), 83.52 (the tenant's duties), 83.59 and 83.67 (how a landlord may get the home back), 83.60 (if sued, and flawed notices), 83.48 and 83.58 (fees and double rent if the tenant stays), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.681 (court orders over damage), 83.595 and 83.49 (rent and the deposit after moving out), 83.505 (notices by e-mail), and 83.57 and 83.575 (notices this skill does not cover). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- A demand for unpaid rent is a different notice (83.56(3)), with a different count that this tool does not do. Say so; these 7 days do not apply to it.
- A notice that only says the lease will not renew, or that a month-to-month tenancy is ending, names no violation: 83.57 or 83.575 applies, not this skill.
- Something said out loud is not this notice. The statute speaks of "a written notice" (83.56(2)(a)). Say no count has started.
- If the tenant wants to move out instead, go to "Moving out" below.

## What the lease adds

Read the clause or rule the notice points to, and set it beside what the notice says the tenant did. Quote it and cite it.

- The lease or a rule forbids it: say so. The lease allows it, or says nothing about it: say that plainly, and ask for any rule sheet the notice relies on.
- The lease's clause on notices to the tenant, and any e-mail addendum: use them under "How it reached the tenant".
- A clause that lets the landlord end the lease with no notice, less time, or no chance to fix: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, from the notice in their hands, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- notice_words: what the notice says the tenant did, and what it demands, copied from the notice. event_date: the date of what it names.
- notice_delivered: the date the notice reached them, not the date written on it. How it came: handed over, mail, e-mail, left at the door, a portal message, a text. If it was left at the door, whether they were home. If mailed or left at the door, notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left, if they can tell.
- fixed_date: the date they fixed the problem, if they did.
- earlier_warning: any earlier written warning, what it was about, and earlier_warning_date.
- rent_since: whether the landlord has taken rent since it knew of the problem, how much of the month's rent, and when it knew.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed a case, and whether they were served court papers.

## Say this in every answer

After any not-settled sentence, and after what to do about a case already filed, say: the notice does not by itself put the tenant out. "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up the home or abandoned it (83.59(3)). The landlord may not lock them out: it "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device." (83.67(2)). If it does, or cuts a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)). The notice still matters: it starts the count, and a tenant who does nothing can be sued. Never tell a tenant to ignore a notice because it has a flaw.

Then say which kind it is, from the notice's words:

- **Fix it:** it names the problem and says the lease ends if it is not fixed within 7 days. "If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (83.56(2)(b)). Go to option 1, then options 2 and 3 if they fit.
- **Lease over:** it says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to leave. "the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises." (83.56(2)(a)). The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Fixing the problem is not a right under this kind. Go to options 2 and 3, and "If the tenant stays". On a notice over intentional damage to the landlord's property, the landlord may also ask a court for an order against more of it (83.681(1)).
- **Only a warning:** it names a problem but does not end the lease or say the lease will end. No count has started. Say so, and that it may count later as "a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)).

## How it reached the tenant

"The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- Handed over: delivered that day.
- Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away ("if the tenant is absent from the premises" (83.56(4))): a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. Give both readings and choose neither, and call both count_days(notice_sent, 7) and count_days(notice_delivered, 7). One: 83.56(4) makes the mailing or the leaving the delivery, so that day. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the tenant; a fix notice's form says "within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (83.56(2)(b)), and a lease-over notice's form says "7 days from the delivery of this letter" (83.56(2)(a)). Acting by the earlier date meets both; say so.
- E-mail: only if the signed addendum in 83.505(1) exists; then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)). Count from the day it was sent. Read the lease.
- A text, a portal message, or an e-mail with no addendum, or left at the door while they were home: not a way 83.56(4) names, and the text does not say what follows from another way. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached them. Give both readings and choose neither. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice and no count has started. The other: it did what a notice is for, and 83.505 leaves room for "any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading the count runs from the day it reached them: call count_days(notice_delivered, 7). Acting by that date meets both; say so.

## Option 1: fix it within the 7 days

"if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." (83.56(2)(b)).

1. **The notice gives the chance.** If it is the "lease over" kind, this option is not open on that notice; say so.
2. **Within the time.** The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Set fixed_date beside it: on or before it, met; say so plainly. Between two dates, it depends on the reading; say so.
3. **Fixed means the thing the notice names has stopped or been put right.** The tenant can tell. A tenant who disputes the charge can still fix it, and that meets the deadline whichever way the dispute goes; say so. Keeping proof of the fix and telling the landlord in writing shows when it happened.

Fixed in time: the landlord may not end the lease on this notice. But: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph." (83.56(2)(b)). Say that in plain words. If the tenant asks until when: count_days(notice_delivered, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, given as "about" that date, since 12 months is not always 365 days.

Not fixed in time: the rule says "the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement" (83.56(2)(b)), and the form says "your lease shall be deemed terminated" (83.56(2)(b)). Whether the lease ends by itself or only when the landlord acts on it, and so whether a late fix helps before then, is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. Go to "If the tenant stays".

## Option 2: the notice does not fit

A tenant can raise these if sued, and can put them to the landlord in writing now. Whether a flaw ends a case is for the court. "The landlord must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice or in the pleadings before dismissal of the action." (83.60(1)(a)). That sentence sits in a paragraph about cases over unpaid rent; whether it reaches this kind of case is not settled. Say so whenever you name a flaw.

1. **No violation.** The rule covers a tenant who "materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations" (83.56(2)).
   - Set what happened beside 83.52's list and the lease. A guest's conduct can count: the tenant must "require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves" (83.52(7)) so as not to disturb, and not "permit any person" (83.52(6)) to damage the property.
   - "material" is not defined. The lists below show which kind of notice fits; whether conduct on a list is therefore material is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, with the tenant's facts beside the word. One: breaking a clear term of the lease is enough, and the statute calls listed conduct "Examples of such noncompliance" (83.56(2)(b)). The other: it turns on how serious this instance was and what it did to others.
   - "reasonable" describes the rule, and is not defined: set the rule beside the word, and state no test.
2. **The wrong kind: lease over, for something the tenant should get to fix.** Set the conduct beside the statute's two lists; neither list is complete ("include, but are not limited to" (83.56(2)(a))).
   - The no-fix list: "destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act" (83.56(2)(a)), fraudulent entry (83.56(2)(a)), or "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." (83.56(2)(a)). Conduct like these: this kind fits; say so.
   - A repeat: "a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)). A written warning about something similar: call count_days(earlier_warning_date, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, and set event_date beside the result. On or before it, this kind fits, even for conduct on the fix list; say so. Within one day of it, either way, say it is too close to tell, since 12 months is not always 365 days. Later than that, this ground does not apply. Whether two events are "similar" is not defined. A spoken warning is not a written one.
   - The fix list: "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary." (83.56(2)(b)). Conduct like these, with no earlier written warning: this kind does not fit, and the tenant should have had the 7 days. Say so plainly. Stopping the conduct now is still worth doing. The notice's words give no right to fix it, but whether the termination holds is the flaw question for a court.
   - Like neither list, such as a first noise complaint or an accident that damaged something: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is of a nature the tenant should get to fix, so the notice should have given 7 days. The other: the lists are only examples, so the landlord may say it is the kind that gets no chance.
3. **The words are missing.** Each rule has its own words. A notice that does not say what the tenant did is not "specifying the noncompliance" (83.56(2)(a)), so it is not the required notice. So too a notice of either kind that gives less than 7 days. A notice with those but leaving out other parts of "substantially the following form" (83.56(2)(b)), such as the warning about the next 12 months: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice. The other: the form need only be followed substantially.
4. **How it came:** see "How it reached the tenant".
5. **A retaliating landlord.** It is unlawful "to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Raise this when the tenant complained to a code office or to the landlord under 83.56(1), joined a tenant group, or did something like the other examples in 83.64(1). They must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and being treated differently in the rent, the services, or the action taken is required (83.64(4)). It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)), and it does not apply if the landlord proves good cause, whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules" (83.64(3)). Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 3: the landlord gave up the right by taking rent

"If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions" (83.56(5)(a)), the landlord "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). There is nothing for the tenant to do; it is an answer to the notice or a defense if sued.

1. **The landlord knew when it took the rent.** Rent taken after the notice was delivered: met, since the notice shows it knew. Rent before: ask what shows the landlord knew.
2. **The month's whole rent.** "a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). Part of the month's rent: not met.
3. **It is over.** Something that happened once and has not happened again: met, and if 1 and 2 are met, say plainly the landlord gave up ending the lease over it. If it has happened again since: not met for the new event. If it is still going on, like a pet still in the home: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so taking rent gives up nothing. The other: taking rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that violation, and only a new one starts over.
4. **Rent from a program.** The rule "does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government" (83.56(5)(c)), but "waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance." (83.56(5)(c)). Only if the tenant's rent is subsidized.

## If the tenant stays

"If the rental agreement is terminated and the tenant does not vacate the premises, the landlord may recover possession of the dwelling unit as provided in this section." (83.59(1)). That is a court case; it does not happen by itself when the 7 days end.

- Costs: "The prevailing party is entitled to have judgment for costs and execution therefor." (83.59(4)), and the winner may recover attorney fees (83.48).
- Double rent: "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). That section speaks of staying "after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58). Whether a lease ended by this notice has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a lease ended by notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of the term, and a lease cut short has not reached it.

If the landlord sues: "Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2)." (83.56(5)(b)). That means paying "into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)), and the court "must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately" (83.56(5)(b)). Paying, or filing that motion with papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)), in time keeps the defenses. A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Say this first when a case has been filed. Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement. Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Moving out

- Leaving does not by itself settle what is owed. "If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord" (83.595), the landlord may choose among the remedies in 83.595, including holding the tenant to the rent. Load wants_to_leave_early for those and for the 7 days' notice with an address (83.49(5)); the next point still holds where it says the choice is the landlord's.
- Whether a landlord that ended the lease itself can still hold the tenant to rent for the rest of the term is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: ending the lease is the choice to "Treat the rental agreement as terminated" (83.595(1)), "thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)). The other: 83.595 applies to any tenant who breached and gave up the home, so the landlord keeps its choice.
- "If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.56(6)). After the move, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying the tenant must be out when the 7 days end, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case or lock them out.
- Telling the tenant to ignore a notice because of a flaw, or saying a flaw ends any case, without the sentence on curing a notice.
- Counting from the date written on the notice instead of the day it was delivered.
- Saying a fix saves the tenant under a "lease over" notice, or that they must leave within 7 days under a "fix it" notice.
- Saying a tenant who fixed it is clear for good, leaving out the next 12 months.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the landlord has taken rent since it knew, or treating part of a month's rent as giving up the right.
- Explaining how to defend a case without 83.56(5)(b) and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Working out when 12 months end except by count_days(the date, 365), writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.
- Stating a test for "material", "reasonable", "similar", or "unreasonable disturbance" that the statute does not give.

tool_calls.name: get_statute_section
tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). answer:
**Short answer:** It isn't settled whether your landlord can end your lease over one noise complaint with no chance to fix it. The law gives landlords two routes. One gives you 7 days to fix the problem. The other ends the lease and gives you 7 days to leave. Your landlord used the second route, which the law ties to things like a "subsequent or continued" disturbance. A single first-time incident doesn't clearly fit that, and the law doesn't say which route a first noise complaint belongs under. Either way, the letter does not put you out. Your landlord needs a court case to make you leave, and it can't lock you out or shut off your utilities. The letter still matters, though, because a tenant who ignores it can be sued. The letter's 7 days run to May 11, 2026.

Has your landlord taken any rent from you since May 1, and if so, how much of the month's rent?

DETAILS

### Is the letter the kind that ends the lease right away?
Yes. It says your lease is "terminated effective immediately" and gives you 7 days from delivery to leave. That matches the "lease over" notice in 83.56(2)(a), which says "the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises."

Fixing the problem is not a right under this kind of notice. The manager handed it to you on May 4, 2026, and a hand delivery is a way 83.56(4) allows. The 7 days end May 11, 2026.

### Did you do something the lease forbids?
Lease §11 says you and your guests "shall keep noise at a level that does not disturb other residents, and quiet hours are 10:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m." The notice names loud music after midnight on May 1, which falls inside those quiet hours. So the landlord can point to a real lease term.

83.56(2) applies to a tenant who "materially fails to comply" with the lease. "Material" isn't defined. There are two readings:
- **One reading:** breaking a clear lease term is enough.
- **Other reading:** it depends on how serious this one instance was and what it did to your neighbors.

### Is "lease over" the right kind of notice for a first complaint?
This is the open question. 83.56(2)(a) allows an immediate-termination notice when the problem is one the tenant should not get a chance to fix. Its examples include "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." It also allows one for a repeat of something the landlord warned about in writing within 12 months. You had no earlier warning, written or spoken, so the repeat ground doesn't apply.

The other route, in 83.56(2)(b), requires a notice giving 7 days to fix the problem. Its examples are unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles, bad parking, and a messy unit.

A first noise complaint is on neither list, and both lists are only examples. There are two readings:
- **Your reading:** a first noise incident is something you should get to fix, so the landlord should have used the 7-day fix notice.
- **Landlord's reading:** the lists are only examples, and a late-night disturbance is the kind of problem that gets no chance to fix.

The statute doesn't say which reading is right, so a court would decide. Whether a wrong choice of notice ends the landlord's case is also for a court. 83.60(1)(a) says a landlord "must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice." That sentence sits in a paragraph about unpaid-rent cases, and it isn't settled whether it reaches this kind of case.

### Does the letter put you out?
No. The landlord "shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except" through a court case, or when the tenant gives up or abandons the home (83.59(3)). If you stay, the landlord has to sue (83.59(1)).

The landlord also "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device" (83.67(2)). If it locks you out or cuts a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees" (83.67(6)).

Don't ignore the letter because of these flaws. The notice starts the count, and a tenant who does nothing can be sued.

### What if you stay and the landlord sues?
- **Court deposit:** You would have to pay rent into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within 5 days, not counting weekends and holidays, after being served (83.56(5)(b), 83.60(2)). The summons will state this requirement. If you miss it, you give up your defenses, and the court "must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately."
- **Costs and fees:** The winning side gets its court costs (83.59(4)) and may recover attorney fees (83.48).
- **Double rent:** The landlord could claim double rent for any period you stay (83.58). Whether a lease ended by notice has reached its "expiration" under that section isn't settled. One reading says a lease ended by notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other says "expiration" means the end of the term, and a lease cut short hasn't reached it.

### Could taking your rent help you?
It could. If the landlord accepts a full month's rent with actual knowledge of the problem, it gives up the right to end the lease over that problem (83.56(5)(a)). Accepting only part of the rent doesn't count. Rent taken after May 4 would show the landlord knew, which is why I asked about it.

tool_calls.result:
Loaded notice_received_violation. Its instructions:

# Notice of a violation

Rests on 83.56(2), (4), (5), and (6) (the notice and how it reaches the tenant), 83.52 (the tenant's duties), 83.59 and 83.67 (how a landlord may get the home back), 83.60 (if sued, and flawed notices), 83.48 and 83.58 (fees and double rent if the tenant stays), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.681 (court orders over damage), 83.595 and 83.49 (rent and the deposit after moving out), 83.505 (notices by e-mail), and 83.57 and 83.575 (notices this skill does not cover). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- A demand for unpaid rent is a different notice (83.56(3)), with a different count that this tool does not do. Say so; these 7 days do not apply to it.
- A notice that only says the lease will not renew, or that a month-to-month tenancy is ending, names no violation: 83.57 or 83.575 applies, not this skill.
- Something said out loud is not this notice. The statute speaks of "a written notice" (83.56(2)(a)). Say no count has started.
- If the tenant wants to move out instead, go to "Moving out" below.

## What the lease adds

Read the clause or rule the notice points to, and set it beside what the notice says the tenant did. Quote it and cite it.

- The lease or a rule forbids it: say so. The lease allows it, or says nothing about it: say that plainly, and ask for any rule sheet the notice relies on.
- The lease's clause on notices to the tenant, and any e-mail addendum: use them under "How it reached the tenant".
- A clause that lets the landlord end the lease with no notice, less time, or no chance to fix: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, from the notice in their hands, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- notice_words: what the notice says the tenant did, and what it demands, copied from the notice. event_date: the date of what it names.
- notice_delivered: the date the notice reached them, not the date written on it. How it came: handed over, mail, e-mail, left at the door, a portal message, a text. If it was left at the door, whether they were home. If mailed or left at the door, notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left, if they can tell.
- fixed_date: the date they fixed the problem, if they did.
- earlier_warning: any earlier written warning, what it was about, and earlier_warning_date.
- rent_since: whether the landlord has taken rent since it knew of the problem, how much of the month's rent, and when it knew.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed a case, and whether they were served court papers.

## Say this in every answer

After any not-settled sentence, and after what to do about a case already filed, say: the notice does not by itself put the tenant out. "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up the home or abandoned it (83.59(3)). The landlord may not lock them out: it "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device." (83.67(2)). If it does, or cuts a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)). The notice still matters: it starts the count, and a tenant who does nothing can be sued. Never tell a tenant to ignore a notice because it has a flaw.

Then say which kind it is, from the notice's words:

- **Fix it:** it names the problem and says the lease ends if it is not fixed within 7 days. "If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (83.56(2)(b)). Go to option 1, then options 2 and 3 if they fit.
- **Lease over:** it says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to leave. "the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises." (83.56(2)(a)). The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Fixing the problem is not a right under this kind. Go to options 2 and 3, and "If the tenant stays". On a notice over intentional damage to the landlord's property, the landlord may also ask a court for an order against more of it (83.681(1)).
- **Only a warning:** it names a problem but does not end the lease or say the lease will end. No count has started. Say so, and that it may count later as "a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)).

## How it reached the tenant

"The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- Handed over: delivered that day.
- Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away ("if the tenant is absent from the premises" (83.56(4))): a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. Give both readings and choose neither, and call both count_days(notice_sent, 7) and count_days(notice_delivered, 7). One: 83.56(4) makes the mailing or the leaving the delivery, so that day. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the tenant; a fix notice's form says "within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (83.56(2)(b)), and a lease-over notice's form says "7 days from the delivery of this letter" (83.56(2)(a)). Acting by the earlier date meets both; say so.
- E-mail: only if the signed addendum in 83.505(1) exists; then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)). Count from the day it was sent. Read the lease.
- A text, a portal message, or an e-mail with no addendum, or left at the door while they were home: not a way 83.56(4) names, and the text does not say what follows from another way. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached them. Give both readings and choose neither. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice and no count has started. The other: it did what a notice is for, and 83.505 leaves room for "any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading the count runs from the day it reached them: call count_days(notice_delivered, 7). Acting by that date meets both; say so.

## Option 1: fix it within the 7 days

"if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." (83.56(2)(b)).

1. **The notice gives the chance.** If it is the "lease over" kind, this option is not open on that notice; say so.
2. **Within the time.** The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Set fixed_date beside it: on or before it, met; say so plainly. Between two dates, it depends on the reading; say so.
3. **Fixed means the thing the notice names has stopped or been put right.** The tenant can tell. A tenant who disputes the charge can still fix it, and that meets the deadline whichever way the dispute goes; say so. Keeping proof of the fix and telling the landlord in writing shows when it happened.

Fixed in time: the landlord may not end the lease on this notice. But: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph." (83.56(2)(b)). Say that in plain words. If the tenant asks until when: count_days(notice_delivered, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, given as "about" that date, since 12 months is not always 365 days.

Not fixed in time: the rule says "the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement" (83.56(2)(b)), and the form says "your lease shall be deemed terminated" (83.56(2)(b)). Whether the lease ends by itself or only when the landlord acts on it, and so whether a late fix helps before then, is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. Go to "If the tenant stays".

## Option 2: the notice does not fit

A tenant can raise these if sued, and can put them to the landlord in writing now. Whether a flaw ends a case is for the court. "The landlord must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice or in the pleadings before dismissal of the action." (83.60(1)(a)). That sentence sits in a paragraph about cases over unpaid rent; whether it reaches this kind of case is not settled. Say so whenever you name a flaw.

1. **No violation.** The rule covers a tenant who "materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations" (83.56(2)).
   - Set what happened beside 83.52's list and the lease. A guest's conduct can count: the tenant must "require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves" (83.52(7)) so as not to disturb, and not "permit any person" (83.52(6)) to damage the property.
   - "material" is not defined. The lists below show which kind of notice fits; whether conduct on a list is therefore material is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, with the tenant's facts beside the word. One: breaking a clear term of the lease is enough, and the statute calls listed conduct "Examples of such noncompliance" (83.56(2)(b)). The other: it turns on how serious this instance was and what it did to others.
   - "reasonable" describes the rule, and is not defined: set the rule beside the word, and state no test.
2. **The wrong kind: lease over, for something the tenant should get to fix.** Set the conduct beside the statute's two lists; neither list is complete ("include, but are not limited to" (83.56(2)(a))).
   - The no-fix list: "destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act" (83.56(2)(a)), fraudulent entry (83.56(2)(a)), or "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." (83.56(2)(a)). Conduct like these: this kind fits; say so.
   - A repeat: "a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)). A written warning about something similar: call count_days(earlier_warning_date, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, and set event_date beside the result. On or before it, this kind fits, even for conduct on the fix list; say so. Within one day of it, either way, say it is too close to tell, since 12 months is not always 365 days. Later than that, this ground does not apply. Whether two events are "similar" is not defined. A spoken warning is not a written one.
   - The fix list: "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary." (83.56(2)(b)). Conduct like these, with no earlier written warning: this kind does not fit, and the tenant should have had the 7 days. Say so plainly. Stopping the conduct now is still worth doing. The notice's words give no right to fix it, but whether the termination holds is the flaw question for a court.
   - Like neither list, such as a first noise complaint or an accident that damaged something: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is of a nature the tenant should get to fix, so the notice should have given 7 days. The other: the lists are only examples, so the landlord may say it is the kind that gets no chance.
3. **The words are missing.** Each rule has its own words. A notice that does not say what the tenant did is not "specifying the noncompliance" (83.56(2)(a)), so it is not the required notice. So too a notice of either kind that gives less than 7 days. A notice with those but leaving out other parts of "substantially the following form" (83.56(2)(b)), such as the warning about the next 12 months: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice. The other: the form need only be followed substantially.
4. **How it came:** see "How it reached the tenant".
5. **A retaliating landlord.** It is unlawful "to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Raise this when the tenant complained to a code office or to the landlord under 83.56(1), joined a tenant group, or did something like the other examples in 83.64(1). They must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and being treated differently in the rent, the services, or the action taken is required (83.64(4)). It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)), and it does not apply if the landlord proves good cause, whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules" (83.64(3)). Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 3: the landlord gave up the right by taking rent

"If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions" (83.56(5)(a)), the landlord "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). There is nothing for the tenant to do; it is an answer to the notice or a defense if sued.

1. **The landlord knew when it took the rent.** Rent taken after the notice was delivered: met, since the notice shows it knew. Rent before: ask what shows the landlord knew.
2. **The month's whole rent.** "a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). Part of the month's rent: not met.
3. **It is over.** Something that happened once and has not happened again: met, and if 1 and 2 are met, say plainly the landlord gave up ending the lease over it. If it has happened again since: not met for the new event. If it is still going on, like a pet still in the home: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so taking rent gives up nothing. The other: taking rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that violation, and only a new one starts over.
4. **Rent from a program.** The rule "does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government" (83.56(5)(c)), but "waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance." (83.56(5)(c)). Only if the tenant's rent is subsidized.

## If the tenant stays

"If the rental agreement is terminated and the tenant does not vacate the premises, the landlord may recover possession of the dwelling unit as provided in this section." (83.59(1)). That is a court case; it does not happen by itself when the 7 days end.

- Costs: "The prevailing party is entitled to have judgment for costs and execution therefor." (83.59(4)), and the winner may recover attorney fees (83.48).
- Double rent: "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). That section speaks of staying "after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58). Whether a lease ended by this notice has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a lease ended by notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of the term, and a lease cut short has not reached it.

If the landlord sues: "Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2)." (83.56(5)(b)). That means paying "into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)), and the court "must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately" (83.56(5)(b)). Paying, or filing that motion with papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)), in time keeps the defenses. A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Say this first when a case has been filed. Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement. Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Moving out

- Leaving does not by itself settle what is owed. "If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord" (83.595), the landlord may choose among the remedies in 83.595, including holding the tenant to the rent. Load wants_to_leave_early for those and for the 7 days' notice with an address (83.49(5)); the next point still holds where it says the choice is the landlord's.
- Whether a landlord that ended the lease itself can still hold the tenant to rent for the rest of the term is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: ending the lease is the choice to "Treat the rental agreement as terminated" (83.595(1)), "thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)). The other: 83.595 applies to any tenant who breached and gave up the home, so the landlord keeps its choice.
- "If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.56(6)). After the move, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying the tenant must be out when the 7 days end, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case or lock them out.
- Telling the tenant to ignore a notice because of a flaw, or saying a flaw ends any case, without the sentence on curing a notice.
- Counting from the date written on the notice instead of the day it was delivered.
- Saying a fix saves the tenant under a "lease over" notice, or that they must leave within 7 days under a "fix it" notice.
- Saying a tenant who fixed it is clear for good, leaving out the next 12 months.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the landlord has taken rent since it knew, or treating part of a month's rent as giving up the right.
- Explaining how to defend a case without 83.56(5)(b) and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Working out when 12 months end except by count_days(the date, 365), writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.
- Stating a test for "material", "reasonable", "similar", or "unreasonable disturbance" that the statute does not give.

answer:
Yes, it changes a lot. Your landlord knew about the fight when it took your full April rent, and the law says that gives up the right to end your lease over that fight. The fight was a single event, and you say nothing like it has happened again. So the termination notice should no longer be good for ending your tenancy over the March 14 fight. This protection covers only that fight. A new incident could lead to a new notice.

The notice also never put you out by itself. Your landlord needs a court case to remove you. It can't lock you out or cut your utilities. If it did, it could owe you damages. You have not been sued, but if you are, don't ignore the court papers, because there are strict deadlines.

One thing could change this: whether a government program pays part of your rent. Does one?

DETAILS

### Does taking April rent cancel the notice?
- The law says that if a landlord "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant," it "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a))
- **Knowledge:** The landlord handed you the notice on March 20, before you paid on April 1. So it knew about the fight.
- **Whole rent:** You paid all $1,050 and the landlord kept it. Taking only part of the rent would not count as giving up the right (83.56(5)(a)).
- **Over and done:** You say nothing like it has happened again.
- Together, these point to the landlord having given up ending your lease over the March 14 fight. You don't have to do anything for this to apply. You can raise it as an answer to the notice, or as a defense if you are sued.

### Is the notice itself flawed?
- The notice says your lease "is terminated effective immediately" and gives 7 days to leave. The statute's form for that kind of notice is nearly the same (83.56(2)(a)).
- You got it by hand on March 20. Handing it over is a delivery method the statute allows (83.56(4)). The 7 days ended March 27, so that date has passed.
- You had no earlier written warning. The "lease over" notice, with no chance to fix the problem, is for conduct the tenant should not get to cure. The statute lists "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance" as an example (83.56(2)(a)). Landlords must give a chance to fix problems like "unauthorized... guests" (83.56(2)(b)).
- A first hallway fight fits neither list clearly. Whether this was the kind that needed a chance to fix is not settled. One reading is that the notice should have given 7 days to fix it. The other is that the lists are only examples, so the landlord can say a fight is the kind that gets no chance.
- Whether the fight was a "material" breach is also not settled. The lease says guests and tenants "shall keep noise at a level that does not disturb other residents" (Lease §11). The statute requires a tenant to make guests behave so they don't disturb others (83.52(7)). The landlord can say the fight broke those rules. You can say one fight was not serious enough to be material. The rent waiver above doesn't depend on how this is resolved.

### What if the landlord tries to remove you anyway?
- Your landlord can recover possession only through a court case (83.59(3)).
- It "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device." (83.67(2)).
- If it did, it would be liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees." (83.67(6)).
- If you are sued, you must pay the rent the court sets into the court registry, or file a motion to set that amount, within 5 days after you are served. Missing that deadline waives your defenses other than payment, and the court "must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant" (83.56(5)(b); 83.60(2)). The summons will state the requirement.

### Is the rent waiver different if a program pays part of your rent?
- Yes. For the part of rent paid by a government subsidy, the waiver rule "does not apply," unless the landlord has not started a court case "within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance." (83.56(5)(c))
- Your lease shows rent of $1,050 and says nothing about a subsidy. That is why I'm asking.
