answer:
Not necessarily. It isn't settled whether the landlord has given up the right to act over a dog that is still in the apartment. Your facts help you, because the manager saw the dog, said nothing, and accepted full rent four times. But the law protects the landlord when a violation is "continuing," and a dog that is still there may count as one. The notice also doesn't put you out by itself. Only a court case can do that, and the landlord can't lock you out or cut off utilities. You still shouldn't ignore the notice. Its 7-day count runs through March 16, 2026. Removing the dog by then meets the notice's demand whichever side is right about waiver.

Is the manager who saw the dog in November the same person who handed you the notice?

DETAILS

### Did taking your rent make the landlord give up its right to object?
- Section 83.56(5)(a) says that if the landlord accepts rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant," it "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance."
- Knowledge: you confirmed the manager saw the dog on November 10, 2025 and said nothing.
- Full rent: you confirmed you paid full rent on the first of each month from December through March, and each payment was accepted. Part payments wouldn't count, but yours were full.
- Whether the manager's knowledge is the landlord's knowledge is a fact I haven't confirmed. The lease names Marsh Creek Property Management as the landlord's agent, and Dana Ortiz signed as its property manager. That is why I'm asking who the manager is.
- The open problem is the word "continuing." The dog is still in the apartment.
  - Reading for you: taking rent with knowledge gave up the right to end the lease over this dog. Only a new violation would start the clock again.
  - Reading for the landlord: a dog that is still there is a "continuing noncompliance," so taking rent gave up nothing.
- The statute doesn't say which reading is correct, so I can't tell you which way a court would go.

### Is the notice itself a proper notice?
- Clause 11 of your lease says: "Tenant shall not keep any pet in the apartment without Landlord's written consent." You haven't told me you have written consent. Silence from the manager isn't written consent.
- The notice is the "fix it" kind. It names the dog and clause 11, and it gives 7 days to correct the problem. Its wording follows the form in 83.56(2)(b), including the warning about the next 12 months.
- Section 83.56(2)(b) lists "unauthorized pets" as conduct the tenant should get a chance to fix. So a notice that gives 7 days fits a dog.
- The manager handed you the notice on March 9, 2026. Handing it to you is a delivery method the statute names (83.56(4)). Seven days from then ends March 16, 2026, and that date hasn't passed.

### What happens if you remove the dog by March 16?
- Under 83.56(2)(b), if the problem is corrected within 7 days of delivery, the landlord can't end the lease on this notice.
- That works even if you think the landlord waived its rights. You wouldn't be admitting anything.
- There is a catch. Section 83.56(2)(b) says: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice." If the dog comes back within that year, the landlord could file without warning you again.
- Keep proof of the date the dog left, and tell the landlord in writing.

### What if the dog stays and the landlord sues?
- Section 83.59(3) says the landlord can't recover the home except through a court case, or if you give up or abandon the home.
- Section 83.67(2) says the landlord can't change the locks or otherwise block your access. A landlord who does, or who cuts off a utility, owes "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees" (83.67(6)).
- If you are sued, you must follow 83.60(2). That means paying the rent the court sets into the court registry, or filing a motion about the amount, within the time the summons states. If you miss that, you lose your defenses, including waiver, and the court must enter a default judgment for removal. The summons will explain the requirement.
- Waiver would be your defense in that case. Because it is unsettled, it carries risk.

Loaded notice_received_violation. Its instructions:

# Notice of a violation

Rests on 83.56(2), (4), (5), and (6) (the notice and how it reaches the tenant), 83.52 (the tenant's duties), 83.59 and 83.67 (how a landlord may get the home back), 83.60 (if sued, and flawed notices), 83.48 and 83.58 (fees and double rent if the tenant stays), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.681 (court orders over damage), 83.595 and 83.49 (rent and the deposit after moving out), 83.505 (notices by e-mail), and 83.57 and 83.575 (notices this skill does not cover). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- A demand for unpaid rent is a different notice (83.56(3)), with a different count that this tool does not do. Say so; these 7 days do not apply to it.
- A notice that only says the lease will not renew, or that a month-to-month tenancy is ending, names no violation: 83.57 or 83.575 applies, not this skill.
- Something said out loud is not this notice. The statute speaks of "a written notice" (83.56(2)(a)). Say no count has started.
- If the tenant wants to move out instead, go to "Moving out" below.

## What the lease adds

Read the clause or rule the notice points to, and set it beside what the notice says the tenant did. Quote it and cite it.

- The lease or a rule forbids it: say so. The lease allows it, or says nothing about it: say that plainly, and ask for any rule sheet the notice relies on.
- The lease's clause on notices to the tenant, and any e-mail addendum: use them under "How it reached the tenant".
- A clause that lets the landlord end the lease with no notice, less time, or no chance to fix: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, from the notice in their hands, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- notice_words: what the notice says the tenant did, and what it demands, copied from the notice. event_date: the date of what it names.
- notice_delivered: the date the notice reached them, not the date written on it. How it came: handed over, mail, e-mail, left at the door, a portal message, a text. If it was left at the door, whether they were home. If mailed or left at the door, notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left, if they can tell.
- fixed_date: the date they fixed the problem, if they did.
- earlier_warning: any earlier written warning, what it was about, and earlier_warning_date.
- rent_since: whether the landlord has taken rent since it knew of the problem, how much of the month's rent, and when it knew.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed a case, and whether they were served court papers.

## Say this in every answer

After any not-settled sentence, and after what to do about a case already filed, say: the notice does not by itself put the tenant out. "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up the home or abandoned it (83.59(3)). The landlord may not lock them out: it "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device." (83.67(2)). If it does, or cuts a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)). The notice still matters: it starts the count, and a tenant who does nothing can be sued. Never tell a tenant to ignore a notice because it has a flaw.

Then say which kind it is, from the notice's words:

- **Fix it:** it names the problem and says the lease ends if it is not fixed within 7 days. "If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (83.56(2)(b)). Go to option 1, then options 2 and 3 if they fit.
- **Lease over:** it says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to leave. "the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises." (83.56(2)(a)). The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Fixing the problem is not a right under this kind. Go to options 2 and 3, and "If the tenant stays". On a notice over intentional damage to the landlord's property, the landlord may also ask a court for an order against more of it (83.681(1)).
- **Only a warning:** it names a problem but does not end the lease or say the lease will end. No count has started. Say so, and that it may count later as "a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)).

## How it reached the tenant

"The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- Handed over: delivered that day.
- Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away ("if the tenant is absent from the premises" (83.56(4))): a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. Give both readings and choose neither, and call both count_days(notice_sent, 7) and count_days(notice_delivered, 7). One: 83.56(4) makes the mailing or the leaving the delivery, so that day. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the tenant; a fix notice's form says "within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (83.56(2)(b)), and a lease-over notice's form says "7 days from the delivery of this letter" (83.56(2)(a)). Acting by the earlier date meets both; say so.
- E-mail: only if the signed addendum in 83.505(1) exists; then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)). Count from the day it was sent. Read the lease.
- A text, a portal message, or an e-mail with no addendum, or left at the door while they were home: not a way 83.56(4) names, and the text does not say what follows from another way. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached them. Give both readings and choose neither. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice and no count has started. The other: it did what a notice is for, and 83.505 leaves room for "any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading the count runs from the day it reached them: call count_days(notice_delivered, 7). Acting by that date meets both; say so.

## Option 1: fix it within the 7 days

"if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." (83.56(2)(b)).

1. **The notice gives the chance.** If it is the "lease over" kind, this option is not open on that notice; say so.
2. **Within the time.** The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Set fixed_date beside it: on or before it, met; say so plainly. Between two dates, it depends on the reading; say so.
3. **Fixed means the thing the notice names has stopped or been put right.** The tenant can tell. A tenant who disputes the charge can still fix it, and that meets the deadline whichever way the dispute goes; say so. Keeping proof of the fix and telling the landlord in writing shows when it happened.

Fixed in time: the landlord may not end the lease on this notice. But: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph." (83.56(2)(b)). Say that in plain words. If the tenant asks until when: count_days(notice_delivered, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, given as "about" that date, since 12 months is not always 365 days.

Not fixed in time: the rule says "the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement" (83.56(2)(b)), and the form says "your lease shall be deemed terminated" (83.56(2)(b)). Whether the lease ends by itself or only when the landlord acts on it, and so whether a late fix helps before then, is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. Go to "If the tenant stays".

## Option 2: the notice does not fit

A tenant can raise these if sued, and can put them to the landlord in writing now. Whether a flaw ends a case is for the court. "The landlord must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice or in the pleadings before dismissal of the action." (83.60(1)(a)). That sentence sits in a paragraph about cases over unpaid rent; whether it reaches this kind of case is not settled. Say so whenever you name a flaw.

1. **No violation.** The rule covers a tenant who "materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations" (83.56(2)).
   - Set what happened beside 83.52's list and the lease. A guest's conduct can count: the tenant must "require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves" (83.52(7)) so as not to disturb, and not "permit any person" (83.52(6)) to damage the property.
   - "material" is not defined. The lists below show which kind of notice fits; whether conduct on a list is therefore material is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, with the tenant's facts beside the word. One: breaking a clear term of the lease is enough, and the statute calls listed conduct "Examples of such noncompliance" (83.56(2)(b)). The other: it turns on how serious this instance was and what it did to others.
   - "reasonable" describes the rule, and is not defined: set the rule beside the word, and state no test.
2. **The wrong kind: lease over, for something the tenant should get to fix.** Set the conduct beside the statute's two lists; neither list is complete ("include, but are not limited to" (83.56(2)(a))).
   - The no-fix list: "destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act" (83.56(2)(a)), fraudulent entry (83.56(2)(a)), or "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." (83.56(2)(a)). Conduct like these: this kind fits; say so.
   - A repeat: "a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)). A written warning about something similar: call count_days(earlier_warning_date, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, and set event_date beside the result. On or before it, this kind fits, even for conduct on the fix list; say so. Within one day of it, either way, say it is too close to tell, since 12 months is not always 365 days. Later than that, this ground does not apply. Whether two events are "similar" is not defined. A spoken warning is not a written one.
   - The fix list: "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary." (83.56(2)(b)). Conduct like these, with no earlier written warning: this kind does not fit, and the tenant should have had the 7 days. Say so plainly. Stopping the conduct now is still worth doing. The notice's words give no right to fix it, but whether the termination holds is the flaw question for a court.
   - Like neither list, such as a first noise complaint or an accident that damaged something: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is of a nature the tenant should get to fix, so the notice should have given 7 days. The other: the lists are only examples, so the landlord may say it is the kind that gets no chance.
3. **The words are missing.** Each rule has its own words. A notice that does not say what the tenant did is not "specifying the noncompliance" (83.56(2)(a)), so it is not the required notice. So too a notice of either kind that gives less than 7 days. A notice with those but leaving out other parts of "substantially the following form" (83.56(2)(b)), such as the warning about the next 12 months: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice. The other: the form need only be followed substantially.
4. **How it came:** see "How it reached the tenant".
5. **A retaliating landlord.** It is unlawful "to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Raise this when the tenant complained to a code office or to the landlord under 83.56(1), joined a tenant group, or did something like the other examples in 83.64(1). They must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and being treated differently in the rent, the services, or the action taken is required (83.64(4)). It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)), and it does not apply if the landlord proves good cause, whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules" (83.64(3)). Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 3: the landlord gave up the right by taking rent

"If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions" (83.56(5)(a)), the landlord "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). There is nothing for the tenant to do; it is an answer to the notice or a defense if sued.

1. **The landlord knew when it took the rent.** Rent taken after the notice was delivered: met, since the notice shows it knew. Rent before: ask what shows the landlord knew.
2. **The month's whole rent.** "a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). Part of the month's rent: not met.
3. **It is over.** Something that happened once and has not happened again: met, and if 1 and 2 are met, say plainly the landlord gave up ending the lease over it. If it has happened again since: not met for the new event. If it is still going on, like a pet still in the home: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so taking rent gives up nothing. The other: taking rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that violation, and only a new one starts over.
4. **Rent from a program.** The rule "does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government" (83.56(5)(c)), but "waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance." (83.56(5)(c)). Only if the tenant's rent is subsidized.

## If the tenant stays

"If the rental agreement is terminated and the tenant does not vacate the premises, the landlord may recover possession of the dwelling unit as provided in this section." (83.59(1)). That is a court case; it does not happen by itself when the 7 days end.

- Costs: "The prevailing party is entitled to have judgment for costs and execution therefor." (83.59(4)), and the winner may recover attorney fees (83.48).
- Double rent: "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). That section speaks of staying "after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58). Whether a lease ended by this notice has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a lease ended by notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of the term, and a lease cut short has not reached it.

If the landlord sues: "Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2)." (83.56(5)(b)). That means paying "into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)), and the court "must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately" (83.56(5)(b)). Paying, or filing that motion with papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)), in time keeps the defenses. A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Say this first when a case has been filed. Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement. Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Moving out

- Leaving does not by itself settle what is owed. "If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord" (83.595), the landlord may choose among the remedies in 83.595, including holding the tenant to the rent. Load wants_to_leave_early for those and for the 7 days' notice with an address (83.49(5)); the next point still holds where it says the choice is the landlord's.
- Whether a landlord that ended the lease itself can still hold the tenant to rent for the rest of the term is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: ending the lease is the choice to "Treat the rental agreement as terminated" (83.595(1)), "thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)). The other: 83.595 applies to any tenant who breached and gave up the home, so the landlord keeps its choice.
- "If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.56(6)). After the move, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying the tenant must be out when the 7 days end, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case or lock them out.
- Telling the tenant to ignore a notice because of a flaw, or saying a flaw ends any case, without the sentence on curing a notice.
- Counting from the date written on the notice instead of the day it was delivered.
- Saying a fix saves the tenant under a "lease over" notice, or that they must leave within 7 days under a "fix it" notice.
- Saying a tenant who fixed it is clear for good, leaving out the next 12 months.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the landlord has taken rent since it knew, or treating part of a month's rent as giving up the right.
- Explaining how to defend a case without 83.56(5)(b) and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Working out when 12 months end except by count_days(the date, 365), writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.
- Stating a test for "material", "reasonable", "similar", or "unreasonable disturbance" that the statute does not give.

If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). (c) This subsection does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government or an agency of local, state, or national government; however, waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance. (6) If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3). Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon. If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required. Public housing tenants or tenants receiving rent subsidies are required to deposit only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible pursuant to the federal, state, or local program in which they are participating.

11. RULES. Tenant shall not keep any pet in the apartment without Landlord's written consent. A guest may stay no more than 14 nights in any six months without Landlord's written consent. Tenant shall park only in the space assigned to the apartment, not in visitor spaces. Tenant and Tenant's guests shall keep noise at a level that does not disturb other residents, and quiet hours are 10:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m.

Landlord: Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, by Dana Ortiz, Property Manager    Date: July 10, 2025
Tenant: Jordan Reyes    Date: July 10, 2025

answer:
**Short answer:** No. Promising to stop the parties probably won't get you another chance on this notice. Your January letter was a written warning about loud parties. The party on March 20 came after it. When that happens, the law lets your landlord skip the "fix it" step and end the lease with 7 days' notice. The letter does not put you out by itself, though. Your landlord has to win a court case before you can be made to leave. You can still raise problems with the notice, and you can ask your landlord to take it back. The landlord doesn't have to agree.

The 7 days count from March 23, the day the manager handed you the letter. That makes March 30 the last day. Your landlord can't lock you out or cut your utilities on that day.

Has your landlord taken any rent from you since the March 20 party, or have you paid any? I'm asking because that could change your options.

DETAILS

### Is this a "fix it" notice or a "lease over" notice?
Your notice says the lease "is terminated effective immediately" and gives 7 days to vacate. That is the "lease over" kind. Section 83.56(2)(a) says the landlord may use it when the conduct is "a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation." It also lists "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance" as conduct that gets no chance to fix.

Here is how your facts line up:
- You told me the January 15 warning was a written letter about loud parties after midnight.
- The party on March 20 was also after midnight.
- Twelve months from the warning runs to about January 15, 2027. March 20 falls well inside that.

Under the "lease over" kind, fixing the problem is not a right. Section 83.56(2)(b) gives a 7-day chance to fix only for the "fix it" notice.

### What does your lease say?
Section 11 of your lease says you and your guests "shall keep noise at a level that does not disturb other residents, and quiet hours are 10:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m." A party after midnight is inside those hours. Section 83.52(7) also requires you to make people on the premises with your consent behave so they don't disturb neighbors.

### Was the notice delivered properly?
Yes, it appears so. The manager handed it to you. Section 83.56(4) allows "delivering a true copy." Your lease, section 8, says notices go "to the apartment while Tenant lives there." You were handed the letter at your door. I see no conflict, but you could raise the point.

### Does the notice have the required words?
It says what you did (a loud party after midnight on March 20, after the January 15 warning). It also gives 7 days from delivery. That matches the form in 83.56(2)(a).

### Can you still push back?
Two points are open:
- **"Material" failure.** Section 83.56(2) applies to a tenant who "materially" fails to comply. The law doesn't define "material." One reading is that breaking a clear lease term, like quiet hours, is enough. The other is that it depends on how serious this party was and how it affected neighbors. A court would decide.
- **"Similar violation."** The law doesn't define "similar." Both events were loud late-night parties, which points toward similar.

If a court case is filed, a notice flaw may not end it. Section 83.60(1)(a) says the landlord "must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice." That sentence sits in a paragraph about unpaid-rent cases. Whether it reaches this kind of case isn't settled.

### Taking rent can matter
Under 83.56(5)(a), if your landlord accepts a full month's rent knowing about the violation, it gives up the right to end the lease over that violation. It does not give up the right to act on a new violation. Partial rent doesn't count. That is why I asked about rent.

### What if you stay past March 30?
The notice does not by itself put you out. Section 83.59(3) says the landlord "shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except" through a court case, or when the tenant gives up the home or abandons it. Section 83.67(2) bars the landlord from changing the locks or otherwise preventing "reasonable access to the dwelling unit." Under 83.67(6), a landlord who locks you out or cuts a utility is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees."

The notice still matters, because a tenant who does nothing can be sued. If you stay and the landlord wins, you could owe court costs (83.59(4)) and attorney fees (83.48). You could also owe double rent under 83.58. Whether double rent applies when a notice ended the lease, rather than the term running out, is not settled.

If you are sued, you must pay the rent the landlord claims into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within the time the summons states. Otherwise you lose your defenses and the court must order you removed (83.56(5)(b), 83.60(2)).

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded notice_received_violation. Its instructions:

# Notice of a violation

Rests on 83.56(2), (4), (5), and (6) (the notice and how it reaches the tenant), 83.52 (the tenant's duties), 83.59 and 83.67 (how a landlord may get the home back), 83.60 (if sued, and flawed notices), 83.48 and 83.58 (fees and double rent if the tenant stays), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.681 (court orders over damage), 83.595 and 83.49 (rent and the deposit after moving out), 83.505 (notices by e-mail), and 83.57 and 83.575 (notices this skill does not cover). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- A demand for unpaid rent is a different notice (83.56(3)), with a different count that this tool does not do. Say so; these 7 days do not apply to it.
- A notice that only says the lease will not renew, or that a month-to-month tenancy is ending, names no violation: 83.57 or 83.575 applies, not this skill.
- Something said out loud is not this notice. The statute speaks of "a written notice" (83.56(2)(a)). Say no count has started.
- If the tenant wants to move out instead, go to "Moving out" below.

## What the lease adds

Read the clause or rule the notice points to, and set it beside what the notice says the tenant did. Quote it and cite it.

- The lease or a rule forbids it: say so. The lease allows it, or says nothing about it: say that plainly, and ask for any rule sheet the notice relies on.
- The lease's clause on notices to the tenant, and any e-mail addendum: use them under "How it reached the tenant".
- A clause that lets the landlord end the lease with no notice, less time, or no chance to fix: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, from the notice in their hands, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- notice_words: what the notice says the tenant did, and what it demands, copied from the notice. event_date: the date of what it names.
- notice_delivered: the date the notice reached them, not the date written on it. How it came: handed over, mail, e-mail, left at the door, a portal message, a text. If it was left at the door, whether they were home. If mailed or left at the door, notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left, if they can tell.
- fixed_date: the date they fixed the problem, if they did.
- earlier_warning: any earlier written warning, what it was about, and earlier_warning_date.
- rent_since: whether the landlord has taken rent since it knew of the problem, how much of the month's rent, and when it knew.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed a case, and whether they were served court papers.

## Say this in every answer

After any not-settled sentence, and after what to do about a case already filed, say: the notice does not by itself put the tenant out. "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up the home or abandoned it (83.59(3)). The landlord may not lock them out: it "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device." (83.67(2)). If it does, or cuts a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)). The notice still matters: it starts the count, and a tenant who does nothing can be sued. Never tell a tenant to ignore a notice because it has a flaw.

Then say which kind it is, from the notice's words:

- **Fix it:** it names the problem and says the lease ends if it is not fixed within 7 days. "If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (83.56(2)(b)). Go to option 1, then options 2 and 3 if they fit.
- **Lease over:** it says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to leave. "the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises." (83.56(2)(a)). The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Fixing the problem is not a right under this kind. Go to options 2 and 3, and "If the tenant stays". On a notice over intentional damage to the landlord's property, the landlord may also ask a court for an order against more of it (83.681(1)).
- **Only a warning:** it names a problem but does not end the lease or say the lease will end. No count has started. Say so, and that it may count later as "a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)).

## How it reached the tenant

"The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- Handed over: delivered that day.
- Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away ("if the tenant is absent from the premises" (83.56(4))): a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. Give both readings and choose neither, and call both count_days(notice_sent, 7) and count_days(notice_delivered, 7). One: 83.56(4) makes the mailing or the leaving the delivery, so that day. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the tenant; a fix notice's form says "within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (83.56(2)(b)), and a lease-over notice's form says "7 days from the delivery of this letter" (83.56(2)(a)). Acting by the earlier date meets both; say so.
- E-mail: only if the signed addendum in 83.505(1) exists; then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)). Count from the day it was sent. Read the lease.
- A text, a portal message, or an e-mail with no addendum, or left at the door while they were home: not a way 83.56(4) names, and the text does not say what follows from another way. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached them. Give both readings and choose neither. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice and no count has started. The other: it did what a notice is for, and 83.505 leaves room for "any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading the count runs from the day it reached them: call count_days(notice_delivered, 7). Acting by that date meets both; say so.

## Option 1: fix it within the 7 days

"if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." (83.56(2)(b)).

1. **The notice gives the chance.** If it is the "lease over" kind, this option is not open on that notice; say so.
2. **Within the time.** The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Set fixed_date beside it: on or before it, met; say so plainly. Between two dates, it depends on the reading; say so.
3. **Fixed means the thing the notice names has stopped or been put right.** The tenant can tell. A tenant who disputes the charge can still fix it, and that meets the deadline whichever way the dispute goes; say so. Keeping proof of the fix and telling the landlord in writing shows when it happened.

Fixed in time: the landlord may not end the lease on this notice. But: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph." (83.56(2)(b)). Say that in plain words. If the tenant asks until when: count_days(notice_delivered, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, given as "about" that date, since 12 months is not always 365 days.

Not fixed in time: the rule says "the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement" (83.56(2)(b)), and the form says "your lease shall be deemed terminated" (83.56(2)(b)). Whether the lease ends by itself or only when the landlord acts on it, and so whether a late fix helps before then, is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. Go to "If the tenant stays".

## Option 2: the notice does not fit

A tenant can raise these if sued, and can put them to the landlord in writing now. Whether a flaw ends a case is for the court. "The landlord must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice or in the pleadings before dismissal of the action." (83.60(1)(a)). That sentence sits in a paragraph about cases over unpaid rent; whether it reaches this kind of case is not settled. Say so whenever you name a flaw.

1. **No violation.** The rule covers a tenant who "materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations" (83.56(2)).
   - Set what happened beside 83.52's list and the lease. A guest's conduct can count: the tenant must "require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves" (83.52(7)) so as not to disturb, and not "permit any person" (83.52(6)) to damage the property.
   - "material" is not defined. The lists below show which kind of notice fits; whether conduct on a list is therefore material is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, with the tenant's facts beside the word. One: breaking a clear term of the lease is enough, and the statute calls listed conduct "Examples of such noncompliance" (83.56(2)(b)). The other: it turns on how serious this instance was and what it did to others.
   - "reasonable" describes the rule, and is not defined: set the rule beside the word, and state no test.
2. **The wrong kind: lease over, for something the tenant should get to fix.** Set the conduct beside the statute's two lists; neither list is complete ("include, but are not limited to" (83.56(2)(a))).
   - The no-fix list: "destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act" (83.56(2)(a)), fraudulent entry (83.56(2)(a)), or "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." (83.56(2)(a)). Conduct like these: this kind fits; say so.
   - A repeat: "a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)). A written warning about something similar: call count_days(earlier_warning_date, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, and set event_date beside the result. On or before it, this kind fits, even for conduct on the fix list; say so. Within one day of it, either way, say it is too close to tell, since 12 months is not always 365 days. Later than that, this ground does not apply. Whether two events are "similar" is not defined. A spoken warning is not a written one.
   - The fix list: "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary." (83.56(2)(b)). Conduct like these, with no earlier written warning: this kind does not fit, and the tenant should have had the 7 days. Say so plainly. Stopping the conduct now is still worth doing. The notice's words give no right to fix it, but whether the termination holds is the flaw question for a court.
   - Like neither list, such as a first noise complaint or an accident that damaged something: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is of a nature the tenant should get to fix, so the notice should have given 7 days. The other: the lists are only examples, so the landlord may say it is the kind that gets no chance.
3. **The words are missing.** Each rule has its own words. A notice that does not say what the tenant did is not "specifying the noncompliance" (83.56(2)(a)), so it is not the required notice. So too a notice of either kind that gives less than 7 days. A notice with those but leaving out other parts of "substantially the following form" (83.56(2)(b)), such as the warning about the next 12 months: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice. The other: the form need only be followed substantially.
4. **How it came:** see "How it reached the tenant".
5. **A retaliating landlord.** It is unlawful "to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Raise this when the tenant complained to a code office or to the landlord under 83.56(1), joined a tenant group, or did something like the other examples in 83.64(1). They must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and being treated differently in the rent, the services, or the action taken is required (83.64(4)). It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)), and it does not apply if the landlord proves good cause, whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules" (83.64(3)). Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 3: the landlord gave up the right by taking rent

"If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions" (83.56(5)(a)), the landlord "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). There is nothing for the tenant to do; it is an answer to the notice or a defense if sued.

1. **The landlord knew when it took the rent.** Rent taken after the notice was delivered: met, since the notice shows it knew. Rent before: ask what shows the landlord knew.
2. **The month's whole rent.** "a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). Part of the month's rent: not met.
3. **It is over.** Something that happened once and has not happened again: met, and if 1 and 2 are met, say plainly the landlord gave up ending the lease over it. If it has happened again since: not met for the new event. If it is still going on, like a pet still in the home: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so taking rent gives up nothing. The other: taking rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that violation, and only a new one starts over.
4. **Rent from a program.** The rule "does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government" (83.56(5)(c)), but "waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance." (83.56(5)(c)). Only if the tenant's rent is subsidized.

## If the tenant stays

"If the rental agreement is terminated and the tenant does not vacate the premises, the landlord may recover possession of the dwelling unit as provided in this section." (83.59(1)). That is a court case; it does not happen by itself when the 7 days end.

- Costs: "The prevailing party is entitled to have judgment for costs and execution therefor." (83.59(4)), and the winner may recover attorney fees (83.48).
- Double rent: "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). That section speaks of staying "after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58). Whether a lease ended by this notice has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a lease ended by notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of the term, and a lease cut short has not reached it.

If the landlord sues: "Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2)." (83.56(5)(b)). That means paying "into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)), and the court "must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately" (83.56(5)(b)). Paying, or filing that motion with papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)), in time keeps the defenses. A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Say this first when a case has been filed. Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement. Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Moving out

- Leaving does not by itself settle what is owed. "If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord" (83.595), the landlord may choose among the remedies in 83.595, including holding the tenant to the rent. Load wants_to_leave_early for those and for the 7 days' notice with an address (83.49(5)); the next point still holds where it says the choice is the landlord's.
- Whether a landlord that ended the lease itself can still hold the tenant to rent for the rest of the term is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: ending the lease is the choice to "Treat the rental agreement as terminated" (83.595(1)), "thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)). The other: 83.595 applies to any tenant who breached and gave up the home, so the landlord keeps its choice.
- "If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.56(6)). After the move, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying the tenant must be out when the 7 days end, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case or lock them out.
- Telling the tenant to ignore a notice because of a flaw, or saying a flaw ends any case, without the sentence on curing a notice.
- Counting from the date written on the notice instead of the day it was delivered.
- Saying a fix saves the tenant under a "lease over" notice, or that they must leave within 7 days under a "fix it" notice.
- Saying a tenant who fixed it is clear for good, leaving out the next 12 months.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the landlord has taken rent since it knew, or treating part of a month's rent as giving up the right.
- Explaining how to defend a case without 83.56(5)(b) and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Working out when 12 months end except by count_days(the date, 365), writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.
- Stating a test for "material", "reasonable", "similar", or "unreasonable disturbance" that the statute does not give.

tool_calls.name: get_statute_section
tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. answer:
**Short answer:** It isn't settled whether they could end your lease over one first noise complaint with no chance to fix it. Florida law lets a landlord end a lease with a 7-day notice and no chance to fix the problem for some conduct. A "subsequent or continued" unreasonable disturbance is one example. Your landlord's notice and delivery appear to follow the form the law describes. But this was a first complaint with no earlier warning, so there is a real argument that you should have been given 7 days to fix it instead. The notice does not put you out by itself. Your landlord needs a court case to make you leave, and can't lock you out. The notice can still be used against you if you ignore it.

My question is: has your landlord taken any rent from you since May 1, and if so, how much of May's rent and when?

DETAILS

### Can they end the lease right away over one party?
- The law lets a landlord act when a tenant "materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement" (83.56(2)).
- Your lease, section 11, says that "quiet hours are 10:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m." and that you and your guests "shall keep noise at a level that does not disturb other residents." Music after midnight on May 1 is the kind of thing that clause covers.
- The law doesn't define "material." One reading is that breaking a clear lease term is enough. The other reading looks at how serious this one night was and what it did to the neighbors. I can't say which a court would choose.
- The law has two kinds of notice. For conduct the tenant should not get to fix, the landlord can say the lease is over and give 7 days to leave (83.56(2)(a)). Examples include "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." For conduct the tenant should get to fix, the landlord must give 7 days to correct it before the lease ends (83.56(2)(b)). The examples there are unauthorized pets, guests or vehicles, bad parking, and keeping the place unsanitary.
- Both lists are only examples (83.56(2)(a), (b)).
- A first noise complaint fits neither list neatly, and that is why this is open.
  - **Landlord's reading:** a disturbance is on the no-fix list, so no chance to fix was needed.
  - **Your reading:** the no-fix example says "subsequent or continued," and this was a single night with no earlier warning. A first complaint is therefore the kind you should get to fix.
- The other way a landlord can skip the fix period is a repeat within 12 months of a written warning for a similar violation (83.56(2)(a)). You told me there was no warning, written or spoken. That route is not available to them.

### Is the notice itself done correctly?
- The manager handed it to you on May 4, 2026. Handing over a copy is a delivery method the law names (83.56(4)). Your lease section 8 also says notices go to you at the apartment.
- The notice says what you did (loud music after midnight on May 1). It says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days from delivery. Those match the law's form (83.56(2)(a)).
- Counting from May 4, the 7 days run to May 11. That date has not passed.
- The lease can't waive these notice rules (83.56(4)).
- If the notice had a flaw, a court would decide what follows. The law says a landlord "must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice or in the pleadings before dismissal of the action" (83.60(1)(a)). That sentence is in a part about unpaid-rent cases, and it isn't settled whether it reaches this kind of case.

### Do you have to be out in 7 days?
- No. The notice does not by itself put you out. "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when you give up the home or abandon it.
- Your landlord may not lock you out. It "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device" (83.67(2)).
- If it does that or cuts a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees" (83.67(6)).
- Don't ignore the notice. If you stay and the landlord sues, the landlord can ask a court to remove you.
- If you are sued, you must pay the rent claimed into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within 5 days (not counting weekends or holidays) after you are served. If you don't, you give up your defenses and the court must order you removed (83.56(5)(b), 83.60(2)). The summons will state this requirement.
- If you stay and lose, the winner can recover court costs (83.59(4)) and attorney fees (83.48). The landlord may also claim double rent for the time you refuse to leave (83.58). It isn't settled whether a lease ended by notice has reached the "expiration" that section speaks of.

### Could taking rent help you?
- If your landlord accepts rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance," it "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)).
- That works only for a full month's rent. Accepting partial rent does not waive the right (83.56(5)(a)).
- It covers only the May 1 incident, not any later one.
- This is why I'm asking about rent. The answer could matter a lot.

Read the clause or rule the notice points to, and set it beside what the notice says the tenant did. Quote it and cite it.

- The lease or a rule forbids it: say so. The lease allows it, or says nothing about it: say that plainly, and ask for any rule sheet the notice relies on.
- The lease's clause on notices to the tenant, and any e-mail addendum: use them under "How it reached the tenant".
- A clause that lets the landlord end the lease with no notice, less time, or no chance to fix: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, from the notice in their hands, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- notice_words: what the notice says the tenant did, and what it demands, copied from the notice. event_date: the date of what it names.
- notice_delivered: the date the notice reached them, not the date written on it. How it came: handed over, mail, e-mail, left at the door, a portal message, a text. If it was left at the door, whether they were home. If mailed or left at the door, notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left, if they can tell.
- fixed_date: the date they fixed the problem, if they did.
- earlier_warning: any earlier written warning, what it was about, and earlier_warning_date.
- rent_since: whether the landlord has taken rent since it knew of the problem, how much of the month's rent, and when it knew.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed a case, and whether they were served court papers.

After any not-settled sentence, and after what to do about a case already filed, say: the notice does not by itself put the tenant out. "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up the home or abandoned it (83.59(3)). The landlord may not lock them out: it "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device." "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

The notice's words give no right to fix it, but whether the termination holds is the flaw question for a court.
   - Like neither list, such as a first noise complaint or an accident that damaged something: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is of a nature the tenant should get to fix, so the notice should have given 7 days. The other: the lists are only examples, so the landlord may say it is the kind that gets no chance.
3. **The words are missing.** Each rule has its own words. A notice that does not say what the tenant did is not "specifying the noncompliance" (83.56(2)(a)), so it is not the required notice. So too a notice of either kind that gives less than 7 days. A notice with those but leaving out other parts of "substantially the following form" (83.56(2)(b)), such as the warning about the next 12 months: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice. The other: the form need only be followed substantially.
4. **How it came:** see "How it reached the tenant".
5. **A retaliating landlord.** It is unlawful "to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Raise this when the tenant complained to a code office or to the landlord under 83.56(1), joined a tenant group, or did something like the other examples in 83.64(1). They must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and being treated differently in the rent, the services, or the action taken is required (83.64(4)). It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)), and it does not apply if the landlord proves good cause, whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules" (83.64(3)). Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 3: the landlord gave up the right by taking rent

"If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions" (83.56(5)(a)), the landlord "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). There is nothing for the tenant to do; it is an answer to the notice or a defense if sued.

1. **The landlord knew when it took the rent.** Rent taken after the notice was delivered: met, since the notice shows it knew. Rent before: ask what shows the landlord knew.
2. **The month's whole rent.** "a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). Part of the month's rent: not met.
3. **It is over.** Something that happened once and has not happened again: met, and if 1 and 2 are met, say plainly the landlord gave up ending the lease over it. If it has happened again since: not met for the new event. If it is still going on, like a pet still in the home: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so taking rent gives up nothing. The other: taking rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that violation, and only a new one starts over.
4. **Rent from a program.** The rule "does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government" (83.56(5)(c)), but "waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance." (83.56(5)(c)). Only if the tenant's rent is subsidized.

## If the tenant stays

"If the rental agreement is terminated and the tenant does not vacate the premises, the landlord may recover possession of the dwelling unit as provided in this section." (83.59(1)). That is a court case; it does not happen by itself when the 7 days end.

- Costs: "The prevailing party is entitled to have judgment for costs and execution therefor." (83.59(4)), and the winner may recover attorney fees (83.48).
- Double rent: "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). That section speaks of staying "after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58). Whether a lease ended by this notice has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a lease ended by notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of the term, and a lease cut short has not reached it.

If the landlord sues: "Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2)." (83.56(5)(b)). That means paying "into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)), and the court "must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately" (83.56(5)(b)). Paying, or filing that motion with papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)), in time keeps the defenses. A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Say this first when a case has been filed. Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement. Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Moving out

- Leaving does not by itself settle what is owed. "If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord" (83.595), the landlord may choose among the remedies in 83.595, including holding the tenant to the rent. Load wants_to_leave_early for those and for the 7 days' notice with an address (83.49(5)); the next point still holds where it says the choice is the landlord's.
- Whether a landlord that ended the lease itself can still hold the tenant to rent for the rest of the term is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: ending the lease is the choice to "Treat the rental agreement as terminated" (83.595(1)), "thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)). The other: 83.595 applies to any tenant who breached and gave up the home, so the landlord keeps its choice.
- "If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.56(6)). After the move, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying the tenant must be out when the 7 days end, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case or lock them out.
- Telling the tenant to ignore a notice because of a flaw, or saying a flaw ends any case, without the sentence on curing a notice.
- Counting from the date written on the notice instead of the day it was delivered.
- Saying a fix saves the tenant under a "lease over" notice, or that they must leave within 7 days under a "fix it" notice.
- Saying a tenant who fixed it is clear for good, leaving out the next 12 months.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the landlord has taken rent since it knew, or treating part of a month's rent as giving up the right.
- Explaining how to defend a case without 83.56(5)(b) and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Working out when 12 months end except by count_days(the date, 365), writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.
- Stating a test for "material", "reasonable", "similar", or "unreasonable disturbance" that the statute does not give.
