answer:
Yes, it changes things in your favor. Your landlord took your full April rent after it had already given you the notice. Under Florida law, that means it most likely gave up the right to end your lease over the March 14 fight. Rent for a later month, or a new problem, would not be covered by that.

The notice also never put you out by itself. Your landlord needs a court case to remove you. It can't lock you out or cut off utilities.

The waiver only covers the March 14 incident. If something similar happens again, your landlord could act on that. Keep your portal receipt for the April payment.

Your landlord has not filed a case, so nothing is pending right now. If you ever get court papers, act on them right away, because the deadlines are short.

Has your landlord said or sent you anything since you paid April rent, such as a message about the notice or the rent?

DETAILS

### What kind of notice did you get?
Your notice says the lease is "terminated effective immediately" and gives 7 days to leave. That is the "lease over" kind of notice under § 83.56(2)(a). That section says the tenant "shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises."

The manager handed it to you on March 20. Counting 7 days from then gives March 27, and that date has passed. Under this kind of notice, fixing the problem is not a right.

### Did accepting April rent waive the termination?
Section 83.56(5)(a) says that if the landlord "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant," the landlord "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." Each part fits your facts:
- **Your landlord knew.** It took the rent on April 1, after it had delivered the notice on March 20. The notice itself shows it knew about the fight.
- **It was the whole month's rent.** You paid all $1,050 and it has not been returned. The statute says only "partial rent" avoids a waiver.
- **It was a one-time event.** You say nothing like it has happened again, so there is no new or continuing problem.

The waiver applies to the March 14 fight only. Your landlord keeps the right to act on a new violation.

### Was the notice valid in the first place?
You may not need this point, but it is a second argument.
- **Delivery.** The notice was handed to you, which is a permitted way to deliver it under § 83.56(4).
- **Your lease.** Section 11 says you and your guests "shall keep noise at a level that does not disturb other residents." A hallway fight could fall under that. Section 83.52(7) also requires a tenant to make sure people on the premises with their consent don't disturb neighbors.
- **Kind of notice.** The statute lists "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance" as conduct that gets no chance to fix it. You had no earlier warning, and this was a single event. The statute also says "material" breaches, but doesn't define that word. Whether one fight justifies a no-fix termination is not settled.
  - One reading is that the landlord should have given you 7 days to fix it, because the listed examples are not complete and this was a first incident.
  - The other reading is that a fight with other residents disturbed is serious enough for the no-fix kind.
- **Curing a defect.** Section 83.60(1)(a) says a landlord "must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice." That sentence sits in a paragraph about unpaid-rent cases. Whether it reaches this kind of case is not settled.

### What if your landlord tries to remove you anyway?
Under § 83.59(3), the landlord may not recover possession except through a court case, or if you gave up the home or abandoned it. Under § 83.67(2), it "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device." Under § 83.67(6), a landlord who does this or cuts a utility is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees."

If your landlord sues, you must follow § 83.60(2) to keep your defenses. The summons will state what is required. In general, you would pay the rent into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within the short time the summons gives. Missing that is an "absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment." Accepting the April rent would be one of your defenses.

Loaded notice_received_violation. Its instructions:

# Notice of a violation

Rests on 83.56(2), (4), (5), and (6) (the notice and how it reaches the tenant), 83.52 (the tenant's duties), 83.59 and 83.67 (how a landlord may get the home back), 83.60 (if sued, and flawed notices), 83.48 and 83.58 (fees and double rent if the tenant stays), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.681 (court orders over damage), 83.595 and 83.49 (rent and the deposit after moving out), 83.505 (notices by e-mail), and 83.57 and 83.575 (notices this skill does not cover). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- A demand for unpaid rent is a different notice (83.56(3)), with a different count that this tool does not do. Say so; these 7 days do not apply to it.
- A notice that only says the lease will not renew, or that a month-to-month tenancy is ending, names no violation: 83.57 or 83.575 applies, not this skill.
- Something said out loud is not this notice. The statute speaks of "a written notice" (83.56(2)(a)). Say no count has started.
- If the tenant wants to move out instead, go to "Moving out" below.

## What the lease adds

Read the clause or rule the notice points to, and set it beside what the notice says the tenant did. Quote it and cite it.

- The lease or a rule forbids it: say so. The lease allows it, or says nothing about it: say that plainly, and ask for any rule sheet the notice relies on.
- The lease's clause on notices to the tenant, and any e-mail addendum: use them under "How it reached the tenant".
- A clause that lets the landlord end the lease with no notice, less time, or no chance to fix: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, from the notice in their hands, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- notice_words: what the notice says the tenant did, and what it demands, copied from the notice. event_date: the date of what it names.
- notice_delivered: the date the notice reached them, not the date written on it. How it came: handed over, mail, e-mail, left at the door, a portal message, a text. If it was left at the door, whether they were home. If mailed or left at the door, notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left, if they can tell.
- fixed_date: the date they fixed the problem, if they did.
- earlier_warning: any earlier written warning, what it was about, and earlier_warning_date.
- rent_since: whether the landlord has taken rent since it knew of the problem, how much of the month's rent, and when it knew.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed a case, and whether they were served court papers.

## Say this in every answer

After any not-settled sentence, and after what to do about a case already filed, say: the notice does not by itself put the tenant out. "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up the home or abandoned it (83.59(3)). The landlord may not lock them out: it "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device." (83.67(2)). If it does, or cuts a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)). The notice still matters: it starts the count, and a tenant who does nothing can be sued. Never tell a tenant to ignore a notice because it has a flaw.

Then say which kind it is, from the notice's words:

- **Fix it:** it names the problem and says the lease ends if it is not fixed within 7 days. "If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (83.56(2)(b)). Go to option 1, then options 2 and 3 if they fit.
- **Lease over:** it says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to leave. "the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises." (83.56(2)(a)). The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Fixing the problem is not a right under this kind. Go to options 2 and 3, and "If the tenant stays". On a notice over intentional damage to the landlord's property, the landlord may also ask a court for an order against more of it (83.681(1)).
- **Only a warning:** it names a problem but does not end the lease or say the lease will end. No count has started. Say so, and that it may count later as "a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)).

## How it reached the tenant

"The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- Handed over: delivered that day.
- Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away ("if the tenant is absent from the premises" (83.56(4))): a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. Give both readings and choose neither, and call both count_days(notice_sent, 7) and count_days(notice_delivered, 7). One: 83.56(4) makes the mailing or the leaving the delivery, so that day. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the tenant; a fix notice's form says "within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (83.56(2)(b)), and a lease-over notice's form says "7 days from the delivery of this letter" (83.56(2)(a)). Acting by the earlier date meets both; say so.
- E-mail: only if the signed addendum in 83.505(1) exists; then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)). Count from the day it was sent. Read the lease.
- A text, a portal message, or an e-mail with no addendum, or left at the door while they were home: not a way 83.56(4) names, and the text does not say what follows from another way. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached them. Give both readings and choose neither. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice and no count has started. The other: it did what a notice is for, and 83.505 leaves room for "any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading the count runs from the day it reached them: call count_days(notice_delivered, 7). Acting by that date meets both; say so.

## Option 1: fix it within the 7 days

"if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." (83.56(2)(b)).

1. **The notice gives the chance.** If it is the "lease over" kind, this option is not open on that notice; say so.
2. **Within the time.** The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Set fixed_date beside it: on or before it, met; say so plainly. Between two dates, it depends on the reading; say so.
3. **Fixed means the thing the notice names has stopped or been put right.** The tenant can tell. A tenant who disputes the charge can still fix it, and that meets the deadline whichever way the dispute goes; say so. Keeping proof of the fix and telling the landlord in writing shows when it happened.

Fixed in time: the landlord may not end the lease on this notice. But: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph." (83.56(2)(b)). Say that in plain words. If the tenant asks until when: count_days(notice_delivered, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, given as "about" that date, since 12 months is not always 365 days.

Not fixed in time: the rule says "the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement" (83.56(2)(b)), and the form says "your lease shall be deemed terminated" (83.56(2)(b)). Whether the lease ends by itself or only when the landlord acts on it, and so whether a late fix helps before then, is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. Go to "If the tenant stays".

## Option 2: the notice does not fit

A tenant can raise these if sued, and can put them to the landlord in writing now. Whether a flaw ends a case is for the court. "The landlord must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice or in the pleadings before dismissal of the action." (83.60(1)(a)). That sentence sits in a paragraph about cases over unpaid rent; whether it reaches this kind of case is not settled. Say so whenever you name a flaw.

1. **No violation.** The rule covers a tenant who "materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations" (83.56(2)).
   - Set what happened beside 83.52's list and the lease. A guest's conduct can count: the tenant must "require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves" (83.52(7)) so as not to disturb, and not "permit any person" (83.52(6)) to damage the property.
   - "material" is not defined. The lists below show which kind of notice fits; whether conduct on a list is therefore material is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, with the tenant's facts beside the word. One: breaking a clear term of the lease is enough, and the statute calls listed conduct "Examples of such noncompliance" (83.56(2)(b)). The other: it turns on how serious this instance was and what it did to others.
   - "reasonable" describes the rule, and is not defined: set the rule beside the word, and state no test.
2. **The wrong kind: lease over, for something the tenant should get to fix.** Set the conduct beside the statute's two lists; neither list is complete ("include, but are not limited to" (83.56(2)(a))).
   - The no-fix list: "destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act" (83.56(2)(a)), fraudulent entry (83.56(2)(a)), or "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." (83.56(2)(a)). Conduct like these: this kind fits; say so.
   - A repeat: "a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)). A written warning about something similar: call count_days(earlier_warning_date, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, and set event_date beside the result. On or before it, this kind fits, even for conduct on the fix list; say so. Within one day of it, either way, say it is too close to tell, since 12 months is not always 365 days. Later than that, this ground does not apply. Whether two events are "similar" is not defined. A spoken warning is not a written one.
   - The fix list: "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary." (83.56(2)(b)). Conduct like these, with no earlier written warning: this kind does not fit, and the tenant should have had the 7 days. Say so plainly. Stopping the conduct now is still worth doing. The notice's words give no right to fix it, but whether the termination holds is the flaw question for a court.
   - Like neither list, such as a first noise complaint or an accident that damaged something: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is of a nature the tenant should get to fix, so the notice should have given 7 days. The other: the lists are only examples, so the landlord may say it is the kind that gets no chance.
3. **The words are missing.** Each rule has its own words. A notice that does not say what the tenant did is not "specifying the noncompliance" (83.56(2)(a)), so it is not the required notice. So too a notice of either kind that gives less than 7 days. A notice with those but leaving out other parts of "substantially the following form" (83.56(2)(b)), such as the warning about the next 12 months: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice. The other: the form need only be followed substantially.
4. **How it came:** see "How it reached the tenant".
5. **A retaliating landlord.** It is unlawful "to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Raise this when the tenant complained to a code office or to the landlord under 83.56(1), joined a tenant group, or did something like the other examples in 83.64(1). They must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and being treated differently in the rent, the services, or the action taken is required (83.64(4)). It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)), and it does not apply if the landlord proves good cause, whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules" (83.64(3)). Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 3: the landlord gave up the right by taking rent

"If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions" (83.56(5)(a)), the landlord "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). There is nothing for the tenant to do; it is an answer to the notice or a defense if sued.

1. **The landlord knew when it took the rent.** Rent taken after the notice was delivered: met, since the notice shows it knew. Rent before: ask what shows the landlord knew.
2. **The month's whole rent.** "a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). Part of the month's rent: not met.
3. **It is over.** Something that happened once and has not happened again: met, and if 1 and 2 are met, say plainly the landlord gave up ending the lease over it. If it has happened again since: not met for the new event. If it is still going on, like a pet still in the home: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so taking rent gives up nothing. The other: taking rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that violation, and only a new one starts over.
4. **Rent from a program.** The rule "does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government" (83.56(5)(c)), but "waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance." (83.56(5)(c)). Only if the tenant's rent is subsidized.

## If the tenant stays

"If the rental agreement is terminated and the tenant does not vacate the premises, the landlord may recover possession of the dwelling unit as provided in this section." (83.59(1)). That is a court case; it does not happen by itself when the 7 days end.

- Costs: "The prevailing party is entitled to have judgment for costs and execution therefor." (83.59(4)), and the winner may recover attorney fees (83.48).
- Double rent: "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). That section speaks of staying "after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58). Whether a lease ended by this notice has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a lease ended by notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of the term, and a lease cut short has not reached it.

If the landlord sues: "Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2)." (83.56(5)(b)). That means paying "into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)), and the court "must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately" (83.56(5)(b)). Paying, or filing that motion with papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)), in time keeps the defenses. A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Say this first when a case has been filed. Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement. Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Moving out

- Leaving does not by itself settle what is owed. "If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord" (83.595), the landlord may choose among the remedies in 83.595, including holding the tenant to the rent. Load wants_to_leave_early for those and for the 7 days' notice with an address (83.49(5)); the next point still holds where it says the choice is the landlord's.
- Whether a landlord that ended the lease itself can still hold the tenant to rent for the rest of the term is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: ending the lease is the choice to "Treat the rental agreement as terminated" (83.595(1)), "thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)). The other: 83.595 applies to any tenant who breached and gave up the home, so the landlord keeps its choice.
- "If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.56(6)). After the move, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying the tenant must be out when the 7 days end, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case or lock them out.
- Telling the tenant to ignore a notice because of a flaw, or saying a flaw ends any case, without the sentence on curing a notice.
- Counting from the date written on the notice instead of the day it was delivered.
- Saying a fix saves the tenant under a "lease over" notice, or that they must leave within 7 days under a "fix it" notice.
- Saying a tenant who fixed it is clear for good, leaving out the next 12 months.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the landlord has taken rent since it knew, or treating part of a month's rent as giving up the right.
- Explaining how to defend a case without 83.56(5)(b) and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Working out when 12 months end except by count_days(the date, 365), writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.
- Stating a test for "material", "reasonable", "similar", or "unreasonable disturbance" that the statute does not give.

tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). (c) This subsection does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government or an agency of local, state, or national government; however, waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance. (6) If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3). History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 23, ch. 82-66; s. 6, ch. 83-151; s. 14, ch. 83-217; s. 6, ch. 87-195; s. 6, ch. 93-255; s. 6, ch. 94-170; s. 1373, ch. 95-147; s. 5, ch. 99-6; s. 8, ch. 2013-136; s. 5, ch. 2025-16; s. 2, ch. 2026-143.

answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to move out because of this letter alone. Your landlord can't remove you without a court case. The letter gives you a chance to fix the problem first, and your 7 days run from March 9, the day the manager handed it to you, not from March 2. By my count, the last day is March 16, 2026. If the dog is no longer kept in the apartment without written consent by then, your landlord can't end the lease over this letter. The letter also warns that if this happens again within 12 months, your landlord can act without giving you another chance to fix it.

Did your landlord know about the dog before you paid March rent on March 1? For example, did the manager see the dog or mention it to you? That could matter, as the details explain.

DETAILS

### What kind of notice is this, and is it valid?
- Your letter is the "fix it" kind. It names the problem (a dog without written consent). It gives 7 days from receipt to correct it. It also warns about repeats within 12 months. That follows the form in Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b).
- Your lease, clause 11, says: "Tenant shall not keep any pet in the apartment without Landlord's written consent." So the letter points to a real lease rule.
- Unauthorized pets are named in 83.56(2)(b) as the kind of problem a tenant should get a chance to fix. You have had no earlier written warning, so this is the right kind of notice.
- Handing the letter to you is a valid way to deliver it under 83.56(4). Counting from March 9 gives March 16.
- School housing doesn't apply to you. You told me this is a private complex.

### What counts as fixing it?
- Under 83.56(2)(b), the problem must be corrected "within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered." Fixing means the thing the letter names has stopped. Here, that means the dog is not kept in the apartment without your landlord's written consent.
- You can fix it even if you think the complaint is unfair. Fixing it in time meets the deadline either way.
- Keep proof of the fix, and tell the office in writing when it happened.
- Clause 11 asks for the landlord's written consent. If you want to keep the dog, a written consent from your landlord would be a different way to meet the clause. Whether your landlord would give one is something I can't tell.
- If you don't fix it by March 16, the statute says the landlord "shall terminate the rental agreement." Whether the lease then ends by itself, or only when your landlord acts, is not settled. Whether a late fix helps before your landlord acts is also not settled.

### Does the letter put you out by itself?
- No. The landlord may not recover possession of the home except through a court case, or if you give up or abandon the home (83.59(3)). Your landlord can't lock you out: it "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device." (83.67(2)).
- If your landlord does that or cuts a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees." (83.67(6)).
- Don't ignore the letter. It starts the count, and a tenant who does nothing can be sued.
- You told me no case has been filed. If you are ever served with court papers, the summons will tell you about a rule on paying rent into the court (83.60(2), 83.56(5)(b)). Missing that step can cost you your defenses.

### Did taking your March rent end your landlord's right to act?
- A landlord who accepts rent knowing about a violation gives up the right to end the lease over it (83.56(5)(a)).
- You paid March rent on March 1, before the letter. The letter itself shows your landlord knew about the dog only from its date, March 2. So whether this rule applies depends on whether your landlord knew before March 1. That is why I'm asking.
- Rent you pay after March 9 would count as taken with knowledge. Whether that gives up the right when the dog is still in the home is not settled. One reading is that a dog still there is a "continuing noncompliance," so taking rent gives up nothing. The other reading is that taking rent with knowledge gives up the right over that violation, and only a new violation starts over.
- Don't rely on this rule. Meeting the March 16 deadline is the safer path.

### What if it happens again?
- The statute says: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice." (83.56(2)(b)). So even if you fix this, a repeat within 12 months could lead to a case without another warning.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded notice_received_violation. Its instructions:

# Notice of a violation

Rests on 83.56(2), (4), (5), and (6) (the notice and how it reaches the tenant), 83.52 (the tenant's duties), 83.59 and 83.67 (how a landlord may get the home back), 83.60 (if sued, and flawed notices), 83.48 and 83.58 (fees and double rent if the tenant stays), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.681 (court orders over damage), 83.595 and 83.49 (rent and the deposit after moving out), 83.505 (notices by e-mail), and 83.57 and 83.575 (notices this skill does not cover). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- A demand for unpaid rent is a different notice (83.56(3)), with a different count that this tool does not do. Say so; these 7 days do not apply to it.
- A notice that only says the lease will not renew, or that a month-to-month tenancy is ending, names no violation: 83.57 or 83.575 applies, not this skill.
- Something said out loud is not this notice. The statute speaks of "a written notice" (83.56(2)(a)). Say no count has started.
- If the tenant wants to move out instead, go to "Moving out" below.

## What the lease adds

Read the clause or rule the notice points to, and set it beside what the notice says the tenant did. Quote it and cite it.

- The lease or a rule forbids it: say so. The lease allows it, or says nothing about it: say that plainly, and ask for any rule sheet the notice relies on.
- The lease's clause on notices to the tenant, and any e-mail addendum: use them under "How it reached the tenant".
- A clause that lets the landlord end the lease with no notice, less time, or no chance to fix: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (83.56(4)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, from the notice in their hands, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- notice_words: what the notice says the tenant did, and what it demands, copied from the notice. event_date: the date of what it names.
- notice_delivered: the date the notice reached them, not the date written on it. How it came: handed over, mail, e-mail, left at the door, a portal message, a text. If it was left at the door, whether they were home. If mailed or left at the door, notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left, if they can tell.
- fixed_date: the date they fixed the problem, if they did.
- earlier_warning: any earlier written warning, what it was about, and earlier_warning_date.
- rent_since: whether the landlord has taken rent since it knew of the problem, how much of the month's rent, and when it knew.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed a case, and whether they were served court papers.

## Say this in every answer

After any not-settled sentence, and after what to do about a case already filed, say: the notice does not by itself put the tenant out. "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up the home or abandoned it (83.59(3)). The landlord may not lock them out: it "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device." (83.67(2)). If it does, or cuts a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)). The notice still matters: it starts the count, and a tenant who does nothing can be sued. Never tell a tenant to ignore a notice because it has a flaw.

Then say which kind it is, from the notice's words:

- **Fix it:** it names the problem and says the lease ends if it is not fixed within 7 days. "If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (83.56(2)(b)). Go to option 1, then options 2 and 3 if they fit.
- **Lease over:** it says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to leave. "the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises." (83.56(2)(a)). The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Fixing the problem is not a right under this kind. Go to options 2 and 3, and "If the tenant stays". On a notice over intentional damage to the landlord's property, the landlord may also ask a court for an order against more of it (83.681(1)).
- **Only a warning:** it names a problem but does not end the lease or say the lease will end. No count has started. Say so, and that it may count later as "a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)).

## How it reached the tenant

"The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- Handed over: delivered that day.
- Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away ("if the tenant is absent from the premises" (83.56(4))): a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. Give both readings and choose neither, and call both count_days(notice_sent, 7) and count_days(notice_delivered, 7). One: 83.56(4) makes the mailing or the leaving the delivery, so that day. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the tenant; a fix notice's form says "within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (83.56(2)(b)), and a lease-over notice's form says "7 days from the delivery of this letter" (83.56(2)(a)). Acting by the earlier date meets both; say so.
- E-mail: only if the signed addendum in 83.505(1) exists; then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)). Count from the day it was sent. Read the lease.
- A text, a portal message, or an e-mail with no addendum, or left at the door while they were home: not a way 83.56(4) names, and the text does not say what follows from another way. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached them. Give both readings and choose neither. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice and no count has started. The other: it did what a notice is for, and 83.505 leaves room for "any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading the count runs from the day it reached them: call count_days(notice_delivered, 7). Acting by that date meets both; say so.

## Option 1: fix it within the 7 days

"if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." (83.56(2)(b)).

1. **The notice gives the chance.** If it is the "lease over" kind, this option is not open on that notice; say so.
2. **Within the time.** The last day: count_days(notice_delivered, 7), or both dates when "How it reached the tenant" gives two. Set fixed_date beside it: on or before it, met; say so plainly. Between two dates, it depends on the reading; say so.
3. **Fixed means the thing the notice names has stopped or been put right.** The tenant can tell. A tenant who disputes the charge can still fix it, and that meets the deadline whichever way the dispute goes; say so. Keeping proof of the fix and telling the landlord in writing shows when it happened.

Fixed in time: the landlord may not end the lease on this notice. But: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph." (83.56(2)(b)). Say that in plain words. If the tenant asks until when: count_days(notice_delivered, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, given as "about" that date, since 12 months is not always 365 days.

Not fixed in time: the rule says "the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement" (83.56(2)(b)), and the form says "your lease shall be deemed terminated" (83.56(2)(b)). Whether the lease ends by itself or only when the landlord acts on it, and so whether a late fix helps before then, is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. Go to "If the tenant stays".

## Option 2: the notice does not fit

A tenant can raise these if sued, and can put them to the landlord in writing now. Whether a flaw ends a case is for the court. "The landlord must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice or in the pleadings before dismissal of the action." (83.60(1)(a)). That sentence sits in a paragraph about cases over unpaid rent; whether it reaches this kind of case is not settled. Say so whenever you name a flaw.

1. **No violation.** The rule covers a tenant who "materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations" (83.56(2)).
   - Set what happened beside 83.52's list and the lease. A guest's conduct can count: the tenant must "require other persons on the premises with his or her consent to conduct themselves" (83.52(7)) so as not to disturb, and not "permit any person" (83.52(6)) to damage the property.
   - "material" is not defined. The lists below show which kind of notice fits; whether conduct on a list is therefore material is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, with the tenant's facts beside the word. One: breaking a clear term of the lease is enough, and the statute calls listed conduct "Examples of such noncompliance" (83.56(2)(b)). The other: it turns on how serious this instance was and what it did to others.
   - "reasonable" describes the rule, and is not defined: set the rule beside the word, and state no test.
2. **The wrong kind: lease over, for something the tenant should get to fix.** Set the conduct beside the statute's two lists; neither list is complete ("include, but are not limited to" (83.56(2)(a))).
   - The no-fix list: "destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act" (83.56(2)(a)), fraudulent entry (83.56(2)(a)), or "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." (83.56(2)(a)). Conduct like these: this kind fits; say so.
   - A repeat: "a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (83.56(2)(a)). A written warning about something similar: call count_days(earlier_warning_date, 365), a stand-in for the 12 months, and set event_date beside the result. On or before it, this kind fits, even for conduct on the fix list; say so. Within one day of it, either way, say it is too close to tell, since 12 months is not always 365 days. Later than that, this ground does not apply. Whether two events are "similar" is not defined. A spoken warning is not a written one.
   - The fix list: "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary." (83.56(2)(b)). Conduct like these, with no earlier written warning: this kind does not fit, and the tenant should have had the 7 days. Say so plainly. Stopping the conduct now is still worth doing. The notice's words give no right to fix it, but whether the termination holds is the flaw question for a court.
   - Like neither list, such as a first noise complaint or an accident that damaged something: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is of a nature the tenant should get to fix, so the notice should have given 7 days. The other: the lists are only examples, so the landlord may say it is the kind that gets no chance.
3. **The words are missing.** Each rule has its own words. A notice that does not say what the tenant did is not "specifying the noncompliance" (83.56(2)(a)), so it is not the required notice. So too a notice of either kind that gives less than 7 days. A notice with those but leaving out other parts of "substantially the following form" (83.56(2)(b)), such as the warning about the next 12 months: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice. The other: the form need only be followed substantially.
4. **How it came:** see "How it reached the tenant".
5. **A retaliating landlord.** It is unlawful "to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Raise this when the tenant complained to a code office or to the landlord under 83.56(1), joined a tenant group, or did something like the other examples in 83.64(1). They must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and being treated differently in the rent, the services, or the action taken is required (83.64(4)). It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)), and it does not apply if the landlord proves good cause, whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules" (83.64(3)). Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 3: the landlord gave up the right by taking rent

"If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions" (83.56(5)(a)), the landlord "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). There is nothing for the tenant to do; it is an answer to the notice or a defense if sued.

1. **The landlord knew when it took the rent.** Rent taken after the notice was delivered: met, since the notice shows it knew. Rent before: ask what shows the landlord knew.
2. **The month's whole rent.** "a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). Part of the month's rent: not met.
3. **It is over.** Something that happened once and has not happened again: met, and if 1 and 2 are met, say plainly the landlord gave up ending the lease over it. If it has happened again since: not met for the new event. If it is still going on, like a pet still in the home: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so taking rent gives up nothing. The other: taking rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that violation, and only a new one starts over.
4. **Rent from a program.** The rule "does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government" (83.56(5)(c)), but "waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance." (83.56(5)(c)). Only if the tenant's rent is subsidized.

## If the tenant stays

"If the rental agreement is terminated and the tenant does not vacate the premises, the landlord may recover possession of the dwelling unit as provided in this section." (83.59(1)). That is a court case; it does not happen by itself when the 7 days end.

- Costs: "The prevailing party is entitled to have judgment for costs and execution therefor." (83.59(4)), and the winner may recover attorney fees (83.48).
- Double rent: "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). That section speaks of staying "after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58). Whether a lease ended by this notice has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a lease ended by notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of the term, and a lease cut short has not reached it.

If the landlord sues: "Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2)." (83.56(5)(b)). That means paying "into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)), and the court "must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately" (83.56(5)(b)). Paying, or filing that motion with papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)), in time keeps the defenses. A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Say this first when a case has been filed. Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement. Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Moving out

- Leaving does not by itself settle what is owed. "If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord" (83.595), the landlord may choose among the remedies in 83.595, including holding the tenant to the rent. Load wants_to_leave_early for those and for the 7 days' notice with an address (83.49(5)); the next point still holds where it says the choice is the landlord's.
- Whether a landlord that ended the lease itself can still hold the tenant to rent for the rest of the term is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: ending the lease is the choice to "Treat the rental agreement as terminated" (83.595(1)), "thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)). The other: 83.595 applies to any tenant who breached and gave up the home, so the landlord keeps its choice.
- "If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.56(6)). After the move, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying the tenant must be out when the 7 days end, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case or lock them out.
- Telling the tenant to ignore a notice because of a flaw, or saying a flaw ends any case, without the sentence on curing a notice.
- Counting from the date written on the notice instead of the day it was delivered.
- Saying a fix saves the tenant under a "lease over" notice, or that they must leave within 7 days under a "fix it" notice.
- Saying a tenant who fixed it is clear for good, leaving out the next 12 months.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the landlord has taken rent since it knew, or treating part of a month's rent as giving up the right.
- Explaining how to defend a case without 83.56(5)(b) and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Working out when 12 months end except by count_days(the date, 365), writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.
- Stating a test for "material", "reasonable", "similar", or "unreasonable disturbance" that the statute does not give.

answer:
**Short answer:** No. The notice doesn't put you out on its own, and the landlord can't remove you or lock you out without going to court. The notice is also probably the wrong kind. The law treats an unauthorized guest as something a tenant normally gets 7 days to fix. Your notice gave you no chance to fix it, and you say you had no earlier written warning. Your boyfriend has moved out, which helps you. Still, don't ignore the notice, because a tenant who does nothing can be sued. Did your landlord or manager know about your boyfriend's stays before the notice? If so, how did they know?

DETAILS

### Does the notice make you leave in 7 days?
- Your manager handed you the notice on April 6, 2026, so the 7 days run to April 13, 2026. That date has not passed.
- The notice says the lease is "terminated effective immediately." That is the "lease over" kind of notice in 83.56(2)(a).
- A notice doesn't remove you. Under 83.59(3), the landlord "shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" through a court case, or when the tenant gives up or abandons the home.
- The landlord also may not lock you out or cut off a utility. Section 83.67(2) says it "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device."
- If the landlord does this, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees." (83.67(6)).
- The notice still matters. It starts the count, and the landlord can sue if you stay.

### Did your boyfriend's stays break the lease?
- Lease section 11 says: "A guest may stay no more than 14 nights in any six months without Landlord's written consent."
- You confirmed he stayed more than 14 nights, and the landlord gave no written consent.
- The statute applies to a tenant who "materially fails to comply with … material provisions of the rental agreement" (83.56(2)).
- "Material" isn't defined. Courts could read it two ways:
  - **Reading one:** breaking a clear lease term is enough. Section 83.56(2)(b) lists unauthorized guests as an example of noncompliance.
  - **Reading two:** it depends on how serious this instance was and whether it affected anyone else.
- It's not settled which reading a court would use.

### Was this the right kind of notice?
- Section 83.56(2)(a) allows a "lease over" notice for conduct the tenant shouldn't get to cure. Its examples are intentional damage to property, fraudulent entry, and "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance."
- It also allows one for repeat conduct "within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation." You had no earlier warning, written or spoken.
- Section 83.56(2)(b) is for conduct the tenant should get to cure. Its examples include "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles."
- A first-time guest violation with no earlier written warning therefore fits the "fix it" kind. That kind requires a notice saying the lease ends only if the problem isn't corrected within 7 days.
- Your notice didn't give you that chance. This is a strong point for you.
- Whether a court would throw out the termination because of this is for the court to decide.
- Section 83.60(1)(a) says "The landlord must be given an opportunity to cure a deficiency in a notice or in the pleadings before dismissal of the action." That sentence sits in a paragraph about unpaid-rent cases. It's not settled whether it applies to your kind of case.
- Your boyfriend has moved out, so the problem has stopped. Under a "lease over" notice that is not a right to cure. It is still worth keeping proof of when he left, such as a written note to the landlord.

### Did the landlord give up the right by taking rent?
- Under 83.56(5)(a), a landlord who accepts rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance" "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance."
- You paid April rent on April 1, before the notice. That is why I'm asking what shows the landlord knew about the stays by then.
- If the landlord accepts a full month's rent after April 6, the landlord clearly knew about the stays by then. Because the stays have stopped, that could count as giving up the right to end the lease over them.
- Accepting only part of a month's rent doesn't count as giving up the right.

### What if you stay and the landlord sues?
- Section 83.59(1) says the landlord "may recover possession of the dwelling unit as provided in this section." That means a court case.
- The winner is entitled to costs (83.59(4)) and may recover attorney fees (83.48).
- Section 83.58 allows "double the amount of rent due" for the time a tenant refuses to leave after "the expiration of the rental agreement." Whether a lease ended by notice has reached its "expiration" is not settled. One reading is that it has. The other is that expiration means the end of the term, and a lease cut short hasn't reached it.
- If you are sued, you must follow 83.60(2). You would have to pay the accrued rent into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, "within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process."
- Missing that deadline is "an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment," and the court must enter a default judgment for removal. The summons will state this requirement.
